questions.question: Pre-Reading: Write on a piece of paper one quality that you think a good human being should have.
questions.answer: Model answer: 'Honesty'. A good human being must be honest, because honesty builds trust between people. If everyone dealt with one another truthfully, there would be far less cheating, corruption and suspicion in society, and people would live together with peace and confidence.
questions.explanation: This pre-reading step activates the learner's prior knowledge about good character, which is the theme of the unit. Any single positive quality such as honesty, kindness, courage, patience or justice is acceptable.

questions.question: Read the text and tick (✓) the correct answer. The text is about:
questions.answer: c) The migration and teachings of Prophet Muhammad (S.A.W).
questions.explanation: The passage recounts the migration (Hijra) from Makkah to Madina, the Charter of Madina and the messages delivered in the Last Sermon, so its overall subject is the migration and teachings of the Holy Prophet (S.A.W).

options.text: The migration and teachings of Prophet Muhammad (S.A.W).

questions.optionsRaw: (a) The battles of Islam. (b) The family of Prophet Muhammad (S.A.W). (c) The migration and teachings of Prophet Muhammad (S.A.W). (d) The last pilgrimage

questions.question: Vocabulary: Find the following words in the text and underline them: ancestors, migrate, aggressive, hypocrites, pagans, harmony, prohibited, alliance, unified, consolidated, astray, beware, superiority, piety, legitimate, equitable, meritocracy, principle. Next, work in pairs and try and guess what the words mean.
questions.answer:
Meanings of the given words:
1. ancestors - persons from whom one is descended; forefathers.
2. migrate - to move from one place or country to another in order to live there.
3. aggressive - ready or likely to attack or quarrel; hostile and forceful.
4. hypocrites - people who pretend to hold beliefs or feelings that they do not really have; false pretenders.
5. pagans - people who worship many gods or idols and do not believe in one God.
6. harmony - peaceful agreement and friendly living together; absence of quarrel.
7. prohibited - forbidden; not allowed by law or rule.
8. alliance - a union or agreement formed between groups or nations for mutual help.
9. unified - joined together so as to form one whole.
10. consolidated - made stronger and more secure; firmly established.
11. astray - away from the right path; into error or wrongdoing.
12. beware - to be careful and on guard against danger.
13. superiority - the state of being higher, better or greater than others.
14. piety - deep respect for God and strict obedience to religious duties; God-fearing goodness.
15. legitimate - lawful and rightful; allowed by law or justice.
16. equitable - fair and impartial to all; just.
17. meritocracy - a system in which people are given position and reward according to their ability and merit rather than their wealth or birth.
18. principle - a basic rule, general truth or standard of behaviour that guides conduct.
questions.explanation: The exercise helps learners infer meaning from the context of the passage and then verify it from the glossary at the end of the book. All the words are used in the lesson about the Holy Prophet's (S.A.W) migration and last sermon.

questions.question: Choose any ten words from the list above and use them in your own sentences. Write these sentences in your notebook.
questions.answer:
Model sentences using ten of the words:
1. ancestors - My ancestors came to this village more than two hundred years ago.
2. migrate - Many birds migrate to warmer regions when winter begins.
3. aggressive - The aggressive crowd refused to listen to the policeman's advice.
4. hypocrites - Hypocrites praise you in your presence and blame you behind your back.
5. pagans - Before the coming of Islam, the pagans of Arabia worshipped idols.
6. harmony - The teacher asked the students to live in harmony with one another.
7. prohibited - Smoking is prohibited in the school building.
8. alliance - The two neighbouring countries signed an alliance to help each other in trade.
9. unified - The captain unified the players into one strong and confident team.
10. consolidated - Hard work and honesty consolidated his position in the company.
(Further examples may be made with: beware, astray, superiority, piety, legitimate, equitable, meritocracy, principle.)
questions.explanation: Using new words in original sentences is the best way to fix them in memory. Any ten of the eighteen listed words may be chosen, but each sentence must show that the writer understands the meaning of the word.

questions.question: Read the text and answer the following question by circling the right answer. How did the Quraish treat the Holy Prophet (S.A.W)? They:
questions.answer: b) opposed him.
questions.explanation: The text says the Quraish 'opposed this new faith so much' and became aggressive, even making attempts on the Prophet's (S.A.W) life, so 'opposed him' is the best answer.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) favoured him. (b) opposed him. (c) loved him. (d) criticized him.

questions.question: Read the text and find out whether the statement is right or wrong: The mission of the Prophet (S.A.W) continued for 23 years.
questions.answer: Right
questions.explanation: This statement is already ticked as the example in the textbook. The Prophet's (S.A.W) mission (from the first revelation to his passing away) lasted for about twenty-three years, so it is a correct statement.

questions.question: Match the part in Column A with the correct part in Column B: Only those people were superior ...
questions.answer: Only those people were superior (f) who led a righteous life. [1 - f, given as the example]
questions.explanation: The Last Sermon says the noblest in God's sight are the most God-fearing. 'Superior ... who led a righteous life' is the match already shown as the example.

questions.question: Work in pairs and complete the statement: Most of the Quraish refused to accept Islam because they thought that the Holy Prophet (S.A.W) was ______________.
questions.answer: Most of the Quraish refused to accept Islam because they thought that the Holy Prophet (S.A.W) was against their gods and their ancestors.
questions.explanation: The text explains that the Quraish thought the Prophet (S.A.W) was against their gods and their ancestors, and therefore opposed the new faith.

questions.question: Work in groups. Orally discuss and then prepare a chart on: The principles that the Holy Prophet (S.A.W) followed after migrating to Madina so that Muslims and non-Muslims could live in peace and harmony.
questions.answer:
Model chart points:
Title: Principles of Peaceful Co-existence after the Migration to Madina.
1. Equality of all communities: the Muslims, the hypocrites, the pagans and the Jews were treated as different but equal groups with definite rights and duties.
2. The Charter (Constitution) of Madina: a written agreement that bound all the communities together for the security of the city.
3. Freedom of religion: every community was free to follow its own faith without compulsion.
4. Collective security: alliances with outside enemies were prohibited so that traitors could not harm the city.
5. Justice for all: all disputes were referred to the Holy Prophet (S.A.W), who decided them fairly, whether the parties were Muslims or non-Muslims.
6. Brotherhood and tolerance: people were encouraged to help one another and to live as one community instead of as rival tribes.
questions.explanation: This group activity asks students to summarise the practical steps the Prophet (S.A.W) took in Madina. The answer is presented as ready-to-copy chart points based on the Charter of Madina described in the text.

questions.question: Pre-Reading: Fold the paper and keep it with you.
questions.answer: Model response: The slip of paper carrying the chosen quality is folded so that the writing is hidden, and the student keeps it safely with him or her until the group activity begins. This keeps the answer secret so that it can be revealed and discussed during the group work.
questions.explanation: Folding and keeping the slip is an instruction that makes the next step (mixing the slips in groups of six) possible. It ensures every student contributes one idea anonymously.

questions.question: Read the text and tick (✓) the correct answer. Which of the following message is mentioned in the Last Sermon, as given in the text?
questions.answer: d) All of the above.
questions.explanation: The Last Sermon clearly states 'Hurt no one so that no one may hurt you', that women have rights over men and men over women, and that 'every Muslim is a brother to every Muslim', so all three messages are present.

options.text: Both men and women have rights over each other.
Muslims are a part of one brotherhood.

questions.optionsRaw: (a) People should not hurt others. (b) Both men and women have rights over each other. (c) Muslims are a part of one brotherhood. (d) All of the above.

questions.question: Read the text and answer the following question by circling the right answer. When did the Holy Prophet (S.A.W) migrate to Madina?
questions.explanation: The text records that the Prophet (S.A.W) entered the city on 2nd July 622, an event known as the Hijra, which marks the beginning of the Islamic calendar.

questions.question: Read the text and find out whether the statement is right or wrong: All the Quraish refused to accept Islam.
questions.answer: Wrong
questions.explanation: The text says that 'most of them refused' to accept Islam, not all of them. Some of the Quraish did accept Islam, so the word 'all' makes the statement wrong.

questions.question: Match the part in Column A with the correct part in Column B: All Muslims were tied to each other ...
questions.answer: All Muslims were tied to each other (g) in the bond of brotherhood.
questions.explanation: 'Tied to each other' is completed by the phrase 'in the bond of brotherhood', matching the sermon's teaching that all Muslims form one brotherhood.

questions.question: Work in pairs and complete the statement: The day the Prophet Muhammad entered Yathrib, marks the start of the ______________.
questions.answer: The day the Prophet Muhammad entered Yathrib, marks the start of the Islamic calendar.
questions.explanation: The entry of the Prophet (S.A.W) into the city on 2nd July 622 is known as the Hijra and marks the beginning of the Islamic calendar.

questions.question: Work in groups. Orally discuss and then prepare a chart on: The basic messages in the last sermon about the rights of other people and why it is important to respect them.
questions.answer:
Model chart points:
Title: Rights of Others in the Last Sermon.
1. Life and property of every person is a sacred trust - so no one may be killed or robbed.
2. Trusts must be returned - 'Return the goods entrusted to you to their rightful owners.'
3. Do not hurt others - 'Hurt no one so that no one may hurt you.'
4. Rights of women - men and women both have rights over each other.
5. Equality of all races and nations - no Arab is superior to a non-Arab, no white to a black; only piety and good deeds matter.
6. Brotherhood of Muslims - every Muslim is a brother to every Muslim, and one must not take another's belongings except with his free consent.
Why we must respect these rights: (i) they protect the weak from the strong; (ii) they create peace and trust in society; (iii) they are for all times, so universal welfare and justice depend on obeying them.
questions.explanation: The Last Sermon lists the fundamental rights of all people - life, property, trust, women's rights, racial equality and brotherhood. Respecting them ensures a just and peaceful society.

questions.question: Pre-Reading: Form groups of six. All the students should put their slips on the table and mix them up.
questions.answer: Model response: The class is divided into groups of six. Each member places his or her folded slip on the group's table. The slips are then shuffled and mixed together so that no one knows which slip belongs to whom.
questions.explanation: Mixing the slips makes the activity fair and impersonal, so that the qualities are discussed on their own merit rather than as the opinion of a particular classmate.

questions.question: Read the text and answer the following question by circling the right answer. When the Holy Prophet (S.A.W) settled in Madina, which of the following groups of people lived there?
questions.answer: c) Muslims, pagans, hypocrites and Jews
questions.explanation: The text states that Madina had four broad groups: the Muslims, the hypocrites, the pagan people of Aws and Khazraj, and the Jews. Hence all four groups lived there.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Muslims and Jews (b) Muslims, pagans and Jews (c) Muslims, pagans, hypocrites and Jews (d) Muslims, hypocrites and Jews

questions.question: Read the text and find out whether the statement is right or wrong: The City of Yathrib was less than 320 miles away from Makkah.
questions.answer: Wrong
questions.explanation: The text clearly states that Yathrib was a city 320 km (200 miles) north of Makkah. It was not less than 320 miles; the given distance is 320 kilometres, which is about 200 miles.

questions.question: Match the part in Column A with the correct part in Column B: The only thing that made one person better than the other ...
questions.answer: The only thing that made one person better than the other (j) was the goodness with which they led their lives.
questions.explanation: According to the sermon, only piety and good deeds raise one person above another, so 'the goodness with which they led their lives' is the correct match.

questions.question: Work in pairs and complete the statement: The Holy Prophet (S.A.W) invited the leaders of all the communities living in Madina to discuss ______________.
questions.answer: The Holy Prophet (S.A.W) invited the leaders of all the communities living in Madina to discuss a formal agreement for harmony among the communities and for the security of the city of Madina.
questions.explanation: The Prophet (S.A.W) wanted all the groups in Madina to live peacefully, so he called their leaders to agree on harmony and the security of the city, which resulted in the Charter of Madina.

questions.question: Work in groups. Orally discuss and then prepare a chart on: At least five teachings, as described in the Last Sermon of the Holy Prophet (S.A.W), that we should practise in our daily life in order to strengthen our society.
questions.answer:
Model chart points - five daily-life teachings from the Last Sermon:
1. Be honest and trustworthy - return anything you borrow and keep your promises, so that people can trust one another.
2. Never harm anyone - avoid hurting others by word or deed, whether in the street, at home or on the road.
3. Treat everyone equally - do not look down on anyone because of colour, caste, wealth or language; respect merit and good character.
4. Respect the rights of women - give women their due honour, protection and the right to be heard.
5. Live as brothers and sisters - help neighbours and fellow citizens in trouble, and do not take what is not lawfully yours.
Practising these five teachings in daily life reduces quarrels, corruption and injustice and makes society strong, peaceful and progressive.
questions.explanation: This activity requires learners to select teachings from the sermon and connect them with everyday practice. The chart lists five clear, workable teachings and their effect on society.

questions.question: Pre-Reading: Pick up one slip at a time and discuss why that quality is good and how it can make life better for an individual and for the society in which we live.
questions.answer: Model discussion points: Suppose the slip says 'Honesty'. Why it is good: an honest person is trusted and respected by everyone. How it makes life better for the individual: an honest person has a clear conscience, enjoys peace of mind, succeeds in his studies and profession, and is never afraid of being exposed. How it makes life better for society: when people are honest, shops do not cheat customers, officials do not take bribes, courts give fair decisions, taxes are paid and public money is used for the people, so the whole country progresses. The group may then repeat the discussion with other qualities such as kindness, courage, patience, justice and forgiveness.
questions.explanation: This is the main pre-reading discussion. The aim is to make students think about the value of good character both personally and socially, which prepares them for the theme of the reading passage, 'The Last Sermon of the Holy Prophet (S.A.W)'.

questions.question: Read the text and answer the following question by circling the right answer. Where did the Holy Prophet (S.A.W) deliver his last sermon?
questions.answer: b) Uranah valley
questions.explanation: The text says the Prophet (S.A.W) delivered his last sermon in the Uranah valley of Mount Arafat on the 9th of Dhu al-Hijjah, 10 A.H.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Quba mosque (b) Uranah valley (c) Jabal-e-Rehmat (d) Hudebia

questions.question: Read the text and find out whether the statement is right or wrong: The Holy Prophet (S.A.W) decided to build a mosque at a place outside Yathrib before entering the city.
questions.answer: Right
questions.explanation: The text says the Prophet (S.A.W) stopped at a place called Quba', a few miles from the main city, and built a mosque there before he entered Yathrib. So the statement is correct.

questions.question: Match the part in Column A with the correct part in Column B: No Muslim had a right to things belonging to other Muslims ...
questions.answer: No Muslim had a right to things belonging to other Muslims (i) unless they gave these of their own free will.
questions.explanation: The sermon states that nothing belonging to a fellow Muslim is lawful for another 'unless it was given freely and willingly', which matches option (i).

questions.question: Work in pairs and complete the statement: The three main points of the Charter of Madina were ______________.
questions.answer: The three main points of the Charter of Madina were: (i) it mentioned the rights and duties of the Muslims and the Jews of Madina; (ii) it gave freedom of religion; and (iii) it prohibited any alliance with the outside enemies (and declared that any dispute would be referred to the Holy Prophet (S.A.W) for settlement).
questions.explanation: The Charter of Madina, also called the Constitution of Madina, laid down the rights and duties of the Muslims and Jews, granted freedom of religion and forbade alliances with outside enemies.

questions.question: Work in groups. Orally discuss and then prepare a chart on: Some of the bad practices that we have adopted, which are against the teachings of the last sermon of the Holy Prophet (S.A.W), and how these are affecting our society.
questions.answer:
Model chart points:
Bad practices against the Last Sermon:
1. Caste, colour and wealth-based pride - treating some people as superior and others as inferior, which contradicts the teaching that only piety and good deeds raise a person.
2. Bribery and dishonesty - officials and citizens take or give illegal money, violating the command to return trusts and deal honestly.
3. Violence and quarrelling - using force over small disputes instead of settling them peacefully, which breaks the rule 'hurt no one so that no one may hurt you'.
4. Disrespect and ill-treatment of women - denying women their rightful place and rights.
5. Taking others' property unlawfully - cheating, stealing or grabbing land, against the teaching that nothing belonging to a fellow Muslim is lawful except with his free will.
Effects on society: distrust among people, weak law and order, rise in crime and corruption, injustice to the weak, and the breakdown of the family and community. The remedy is to study the Last Sermon again and practise it sincerely.
questions.explanation: This activity develops critical thinking: students identify present-day social evils and measure them against the teachings of the Last Sermon, then suggest the remedy of returning to those teachings.

questions.question: Read the text and answer the following question by circling the right answer. When did the Holy Prophet (S.A.W) perform his last Hajj?
questions.answer: c) 10th year of Hijra
questions.explanation: The passage states that in the year 10 A.H. the Prophet (S.A.W) undertook his farewell pilgrimage to Makkah, in which he delivered the Last Sermon on 9 Dhu al-Hijjah.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) 06th year of Hijra (b) 08th year of Hijra (c) 10th year of Hijra (d) 12th year of Hijra

questions.question: Read the text and find out whether the statement is right or wrong: Today, Yathrib is called Madinat an-Nabi.
questions.answer: Right
questions.explanation: The text says Yathrib was renamed Madinat un-Nabi ('City of the Prophet'), and later the 'un-Nabi' was dropped and it came to be called 'Madina', meaning 'the city'. So Yathrib is indeed the Prophet's city.

questions.question: Match the part in Column A with the correct part in Column B: Satan will try to misguide you in small matters ...
questions.answer: Satan will try to misguide you in small matters (h) so be careful.
questions.explanation: The Prophet (S.A.W) warned the people to be careful of Satan in small things, as he had lost hope of misguiding them in big matters. Hence the match is (h) 'so be careful'.

questions.question: Work in pairs and complete the statement: In order to strengthen the position of the Muslims in Madina, the Holy Prophet (S.A.W) took three major steps, which were ______________.
questions.answer: In order to strengthen the position of the Muslims in Madina, the Holy Prophet (S.A.W) took three major steps, which were: (i) he unified the different Arab tribes under Islam; (ii) he carried out social and religious reforms; and (iii) he made administrative developments that further consolidated the Islamic community in Madina.
questions.explanation: The text states these three measures: unifying the Arab tribes under Islam, social and religious reforms, and administrative developments.

questions.question: Read the text and find out whether the statement is right or wrong: The people of Madina agreed that Prophet Muhammad (S.A.W) should settle their disputes.
questions.answer: Right
questions.explanation: The Charter of Madina 'declared that any dispute would be referred to Prophet Muhammad (S.A.W) for settlement', which shows the people of Madina agreed to this arrangement.

questions.question: Match the part in Column A with the correct part in Column B: Therefore, all claims to superiority ...
questions.answer: Therefore, all claims to superiority (b) that were based on blood and wealth were useless.
questions.explanation: The sermon says false claims to greatness founded on blood or wealth should be crushed, so claims based on blood and wealth are worthless. This matches option (b).

questions.question: Work in pairs and complete the statement: The farewell pilgrimage of the Holy Prophet (S.A.W) is an important event for the Muslims because ______________.
questions.answer: The farewell pilgrimage of the Holy Prophet (S.A.W) is an important event for the Muslims because it was the first and the last pilgrimage made by him, and it was also the occasion when he taught Muslims how to perform the Hajj and delivered his last sermon.
questions.explanation: The text explains that the farewell pilgrimage was significant as the Prophet's (S.A.W) first and last Hajj, during which he taught the rites of Hajj and gave the Last Sermon.

questions.question: Read the text and find out whether the statement is right or wrong: The Holy Prophet (S.A.W) addressed such a large gathering of Muslims for the last time at Arafat.
questions.answer: Right
questions.explanation: During the farewell pilgrimage, the Prophet (S.A.W) delivered his Last Sermon in the Uranah valley of Mount Arafat before a countless gathering of Muslims. It was the last time he addressed such a large gathering.

questions.question: Match the part in Column A with the correct part in Column B: Return all things kept with you in trust ...
questions.answer: Return all things kept with you in trust (a) to the people to whom they belong.
questions.explanation: The sermon instructs that goods entrusted to a person must be returned to their rightful owners, which matches option (a).

questions.question: Work in pairs and complete the statement: The Holy Prophet (S.A.W) asked the people in the gathering to listen carefully as ______________.
questions.answer: The Holy Prophet (S.A.W) asked the people in the gathering to listen carefully as he said that he did not know whether, after that year, he would ever be among them again; therefore they should listen to his words very carefully and take them to those who could not be present.
questions.explanation: The sermon opens with the Prophet (S.A.W) telling the people that he might not live to address them again, so they must listen attentively and pass on his message to others.

questions.question: Read the text and find out whether the statement is right or wrong: Islam has different laws for the black and for the white people.
questions.answer: Wrong
questions.explanation: The Last Sermon says 'a white has no superiority over a black, nor does a black have any superiority over a white, except by piety and good action'. Islam therefore treats all races equally, so the statement is wrong.

questions.question: Match the part in Column A with the correct part in Column B: Both men and women ...
questions.answer: Both men and women (d) have rights over each other.
questions.explanation: The sermon says that although men have rights over their women, the women also have rights over them. Thus 'have rights over each other' matches option (d).

questions.question: Work in pairs and complete the statement: The Muslims can ensure that all people get their fair share by ______________.
questions.answer: The Muslims can ensure that all people get their fair share by following the messages of the Last Sermon - that is, by believing in the equality of all human beings, returning goods held in trust, not hurting others, respecting the rights of one another, and making honesty, justice and meritocracy the guiding principles of society.
questions.explanation: The text concludes that if Muslims follow the messages of the Last Sermon, there will be a fair and equitable society in which honesty, justice and meritocracy prevail.

questions.question: Read the text and find out whether the statement is right or wrong: All human beings are children of Adam and Adam was created from dust.
questions.answer: Right
questions.explanation: The Last Sermon states 'All mankind is from Adam and Adam was created from dust', which is exactly what this statement says, so it is correct.

questions.question: Match the part in Column A with the correct part in Column B: If you will hurt others ...
questions.answer: If you will hurt others (c) you may get hurt in return.
questions.explanation: The sermon warns 'Hurt no one so that no one may hurt you', which expresses the same idea as option (c) 'you may get hurt in return'.

questions.question: Read the text and find out whether the statement is right or wrong: Only the people who heard the last sermon were supposed to follow it.
questions.answer: Wrong
questions.explanation: The Prophet (S.A.W) asked those present to 'take these words to those who could not be present', and the text says the messages of the sermon 'are for all times'. Thus everyone, not only those who heard it, must follow it.

questions.question: Match the part in Column A with the correct part in Column B: Consider the life and property of every Muslim ...
questions.answer: Consider the life and property of every Muslim (e) as a sacred trust.
questions.explanation: The sermon says to regard the life and property of every Muslim as a sacred trust, so option (e) is the correct match.

questions.question: Discussion Topic 1: Some unfair means that students use in exams.
questions.answer:
Model discussion points / presentation:
Theme: Unfair means (cheating) in examinations.
1. Copying from a nearby candidate or from hidden notes ('cheating chits').
2. Carrying smart phones, Bluetooth devices or micro-earpieces into the hall.
3. Getting the question paper or answers in advance through leaked papers.
4. Writing answers on the desk, arm, water bottle or ruler.
5. Hiring an impersonator ('regular' student) to sit the exam in one's place.
6. Asking the invigilator for help, or bribing the staff for extra time or leniency.
7. Passing answers to one another through hand signals or slips.
Presentation tips: divide these points among the speakers, give one real example of each, and end by asking the class which of these practices they have seen and how it can be stopped.
questions.explanation: The listening-and-speaking exercise asks groups to discuss a topic and present it. This topic lists the common unfair means used in examinations - the concrete points the group can note, discuss and present.

questions.question: Discussion Topic 2: Reasons for using unfair means in exams.
questions.answer:
Model discussion points / presentation:
Theme: Why students cheat in examinations.
1. Fear of failure and of disappointing parents, who demand very high marks.
2. Poor preparation - wasting the whole year and then trying to cover up in a few days.
3. Lack of understanding of the subject because of weak teaching, large classes or a difficult syllabus.
4. Competition and the race for marks and admission to good colleges.
5. Laziness and the habit of taking the easy way out.
6. Pressure from friends who are already cheating ('everyone is doing it').
7. Loopholes in the examination system - weak invigilation and delayed or lenient punishment.
8. Financial and family pressures that make students feel that one failure will ruin their future.
Presentation tips: give each reason a short example and suggest that the class discuss which reasons are within the student's own control.
questions.explanation: Understanding the causes of cheating is the first step to stopping it. The group is expected to brainstorm and present the main reasons, then discuss how each can be removed.

questions.question: Discussion Topic 3: Impact of using unfair means in exams on students' performance.
questions.answer:
Model discussion points / presentation:
Theme: How cheating affects the cheater's own performance and learning.
1. Weak foundation - a student who copies never learns the basics, so the next year's course becomes even harder.
2. Poor results in real tests - he cannot cheat in every exam, interview or practical exam, so he fails when it matters.
3. Loss of confidence and self-respect - a cheater knows that his success is hollow and lives in constant fear of being caught.
4. Bad study habits - he stops making the effort to read, memorise and solve problems.
5. Mental stress and anxiety - the fear of detection harms concentration and health.
6. Wrong feedback - copied marks mislead teachers and parents, who cannot see the student's real weaknesses and so cannot help him.
Presentation tips: contrast the cheater with an honest student and show how honest study builds skills that last a lifetime.
questions.explanation: This topic examines the personal cost of cheating on the students' own learning. The points show that unfair means give short-term marks but long-term damage to knowledge, skill and confidence.

questions.question: Discussion Topic 4: Effect of using unfair means on the future of students.
questions.answer:
Model discussion points / presentation:
Theme: Long-term effects of cheating on a student's future.
1. Incompetent professionals - a doctor, engineer, pilot or teacher who cheated through studies may one day harm or endanger the lives of others.
2. Loss of jobs and reputation when the truth is discovered, which can even lead to blacklisting or legal action.
3. Difficulty in higher studies and competitive examinations where real knowledge is required.
4. Weak national productivity - a cheating generation cannot build a strong country.
5. Moral decay - cheating spreads dishonesty to offices, business and politics, increasing corruption.
6. Broken self-confidence and a bad habit of reaching for shortcuts all through life.
Conclusion of the group's talk: Examination dishonesty destroys the very future a student is trying to protect; honest effort is the only safe road to success.
questions.explanation: This topic widens the discussion from the examination hall to adult life and national progress, showing that cheating produces a weak, dishonest and unproductive generation.

questions.question: Find the correct match from Column B and write it in the answer column: If all people in Pakistan became honest ...
questions.answer: If all people in Pakistan became honest (g) the country would progress very fast. [1 - g, given as the example]
questions.explanation: In a second conditional sentence an imaginary present situation (if + simple past) is followed by 'would + verb'. Honesty everywhere would lead to fast progress, so 1 matches g.

questions.question: Complete the second conditional sentence by using the correct form of the verb in brackets: a) If she studied harder, _____________ (get).
questions.answer: If she studied harder, she would get good marks.
questions.explanation: In a second conditional the main clause uses 'would + base verb'. 'Get' becomes 'would get'.

questions.question: Complete the following dialogue by using some or all of the words given below (want, have, come, fall, sick, join, swim, go, plan, be). You may use your own words or use these words any number of times.
questions.answer:
(Completed dialogue)
Zahid: We had to call off our picnic plan. First, we decided to go to the seaside but we could not do so.
Qasim: Why?
Zahid: If we went to the sea side, Salim would not come.
Qasim: Why would Salim not come?
Zahid: If we went swimming, he would fall sick.
Qasim: You don't fall sick when you swim.
Zahid: Salim's heart is weak. He would be sick, if he swam.
Qasim: You could have gone to the park.
Zahid: Tahir and Salman said that if we went to the park, they would join us.
Qasim: Then what?
Zahid: Someone suggested that we visit the museum. However, half the group objected and said that if we went there, they would not come.
Qasim: Why?
Zahid: They said that they would have fun themselves, if we just came along.
Qasim: They were right. If you want to have fun, then you have that inside the museum.
Zahid: So, if we wanted to please everyone, we would be unable to settle on a place to go, hence, the plan was dropped.
questions.explanation: This guided dialogue practises the second conditional in a natural conversation. The words in bold (swimming/fall, be/sick, went/join, went/come, have/came, want/have, wanted/be) are the given verbs used in their correct second-conditional forms. The last blank may also be completed as '...we would plan a place to go...'.

questions.question: Revision: Punctuation. Work in pairs and correct the punctuation and capitalization in the passage 'Forming Habits'. Put capital letters, full stops, question marks, commas and apostrophes where they are needed.
questions.answer:
(Corrected passage)
Forming Habits

How long does it take to form a new habit? I looked for an answer the same way most people do nowadays; I asked Google. The answer I got was 21 days. It seemed that if you repeat a behaviour every day for 21 days, you can form a brand-new habit. Then I asked, "Can one change all types of behaviour in 21 days, or just some types?" I was not able to find an answer. All I could find out was that if it were exercise, smoking, writing a diary, or turning cartwheels, you could do it in 21 days. The important thing was to maintain a chain of 21 days without breaking it.

One psychologist, Mr Mohan, decided to do some research to find out if all new habits could be formed in just 21 days. About 100 people from the Multan University participated in the research. They were asked to choose a behaviour that they wanted to turn into a habit. They all had to choose something they did not already do that could be repeated every day. What do you think the result was?

The results showed that on average it took 66 days until a habit was formed. However, this does not mean that people weren't able to form new habits in 21 days. According to the study findings, some habits could be formed in 21 days, while some could take as long as 254 days. So, 21 days to form a habit is probably right, as long as all you want to do is drink a glass of water after breakfast. Anything harder is likely to take longer to become a really strong habit, and in the case of some activities much longer.
questions.explanation: The exercise revises punctuation and capitalization: the first word of every sentence is capitalised; every statement ends with a full stop; direct questions end with a question mark; commas separate items in a list and clauses; a colon or semicolon may separate closely related ideas; and the apostrophe is used in contractions such as 'wasn't', 'weren't' and 'don't'.

questions.question: Find the correct match from Column B and write it in the answer column: I could easily get an A grade in my exams ...
questions.answer: I could easily get an A grade in my exams (f) if I worked really hard.
questions.explanation: The 'if' clause can also come at the end of the sentence. 'Could get' (imaginary ability) is followed by 'if I worked really hard', so 2 matches f.

questions.question: Complete the second conditional sentence by using the correct form of the verb in brackets: b) If you grew multiple crops on your land, _____________ (earn).
questions.answer: If you grew multiple crops on your land, you would earn more money.
questions.explanation: The imaginary condition 'grew multiple crops' is followed by the result 'would earn'. 'Earn' becomes 'would earn'.

questions.question: Find the correct match from Column B and write it in the answer column: If our driver did not drive so fast ...
questions.answer: If our driver did not drive so fast (d) we would not be in hospital right now.
questions.explanation: Fast driving is the imaginary cause of the accident; the imaginary present result is 'we would not be in hospital right now'. So 3 matches d.

questions.question: Complete the second conditional sentence by using the correct form of the verb in brackets: c) People would fly, _____________ (have).
questions.answer: People would fly, if they had wings.
questions.explanation: Here the 'if' clause comes at the end and uses the simple past 'had'. 'Have' becomes 'had'.

questions.question: Find the correct match from Column B and write it in the answer column: The tourists would not be lost ...
questions.answer: The tourists would not be lost (b) if they had an updated map of the area.
questions.explanation: The imaginary cause is having an updated map; the result is not getting lost. Thus 4 matches b.

questions.question: Complete the second conditional sentence by using the correct form of the verb in brackets: d) If I owned a camera, _____________ (take).
questions.answer: If I owned a camera, I would take photographs of everything I saw.
questions.explanation: The result clause uses 'would + base verb', so 'take' becomes 'would take'.

questions.question: Find the correct match from Column B and write it in the answer column: If they had the time ...
questions.answer: If they had the time (c) they could visit all their friends.
questions.explanation: Having time (imaginary) would let them visit their friends using the modal 'could'. So 5 matches c.

questions.question: Complete the second conditional sentence by using the correct form of the verb in brackets: e) They might win the match, _____________ (work).
questions.answer: They might win the match, if they worked harder.
questions.explanation: The modal 'might' can replace 'would' in the main clause, while the 'if' clause stays in the simple past. 'Work' becomes 'worked'.

questions.question: Find the correct match from Column B and write it in the answer column: If money grew on trees ...
questions.answer: If money grew on trees (h) everyone would be rich.
questions.explanation: An impossible imaginary condition (money growing on trees) would make everyone rich. So 6 matches h.

questions.question: Complete the second conditional sentence by using the correct form of the verb in brackets: f) If Abdullah lived with his family, _____________ (save).
questions.answer: If Abdullah lived with his family, he would save a lot of money.
questions.explanation: The imaginary condition 'lived with his family' leads to the result 'would save'. 'Save' becomes 'would save'.

questions.question: Find the correct match from Column B and write it in the answer column: Our schools would produce capable leaders ...
questions.answer: Our schools would produce capable leaders (a) if the students and teachers paid due attention.
questions.explanation: The imaginary result (capable leaders) depends on the imaginary cause of students and teachers paying due attention. So 7 matches a.

questions.question: Complete the second conditional sentence by using the correct form of the verb in brackets: g) My family would move to the city, _____________ (allow).
questions.answer: My family would move to the city, if we were allowed.
questions.explanation: The passive 'if we were allowed' is used in the 'if' clause, and in a second conditional 'were' is often used instead of 'was'.

questions.question: Find the correct match from Column B and write it in the answer column: Her idea would be accepted ...
questions.answer: Her idea would be accepted (e) if she presented it well.
questions.explanation: The result 'would be accepted' matches the condition 'if she presented it well'. So 8 matches e.

questions.question: Complete the second conditional sentence by using the correct form of the verb in brackets: h) She could become a good doctor, _____________ (get).
questions.answer: She could become a good doctor, if she got admission to a medical college.
questions.explanation: The modal 'could' replaces 'would' in the main clause and the 'if' clause uses the simple past. 'Get' becomes 'got'.

questions.question: Read the essay 'Deserts'. Discuss the introductory paragraph. Is the thesis statement at the end of the paragraph given in one sentence or two sentences? The thesis statement should contain all the key ideas that are covered in the essay.
questions.answer: Model response: The introductory paragraph begins by saying that it is difficult to imagine a desert without having seen one, then defines a desert (a vast plain of sands and stones, with mountains, hills and few roads), mentions the springs of water that create green spots and oases, and finally names the Sahara as one of the most remarkable deserts of the world. The thesis statement is given in one sentence - the last sentence of the paragraph ('One of the most remarkable deserts of the world is the Sahara Desert.') - which captures the main idea developed in the body of the essay. The earlier sentences give the general description (moving from general to specific) and lead the reader towards this main idea.
questions.explanation: A descriptive essay's introduction moves from general to specific and ends with a thesis statement. In 'Deserts' the thesis is a single sentence about the Sahara, and the rest of the introduction provides the general description that supports it.

questions.question: Write a descriptive essay of at least four paragraphs on any one of the following topics: (1) My village/town/city.
questions.answer:
(Model descriptive essay)
My Village

My village, Chak No. 47, is a small and beautiful settlement situated about twenty kilometres from the district town. It is surrounded by green fields of wheat, sugarcane and cotton, and a canal flows along its eastern side, giving life to the whole area. Although it is small, there is hardly any place I love more than my village.

The houses of my village are simple but neat. Most of them are made of baked bricks and mud, with wide courtyards and flat roofs where families sleep on hot summer nights. A few new houses have been built with concrete and paint. The streets are narrow and often dusty, but the people keep them clean. At the centre of the village stands the ancient banyan tree, under whose cool shade the village elders gather every evening to talk and to settle small disputes.

The life of the village moves with the seasons. In spring the fields are full of yellow flowers, and the air is sweet with the smell of growing crops. In summer the men work hard all day in the fields and rest in the shade at noon, while in winter the villagers gather around small fires, roasting maize and telling stories. The biggest joys of the year are the two Eids, when the whole village celebrates together, and the harvest festival, when everyone shares the first grain.

To conclude, my village may lack the shops, roads and bright lights of a big city, but it has something far more precious - fresh air, pure water, simple food and warm-hearted people. In the city people live near one another but hardly know each other; in my village everyone is a friend and a helper. I am proud of my village and would never exchange its peace for the noise of the town.
questions.explanation: This is a complete four-paragraph descriptive essay. It follows the model of 'Deserts': a general-to-specific introduction ending with a thesis statement, two body paragraphs each opening with a topic sentence and developed with details, and a conclusion beginning with the signalling phrase 'To conclude'.

questions.question: Analyse the two letters to the editor: (a) To which newspaper's editor were these letters written?
questions.answer: Letter 1 was written to the editor of 'Daily Dawn', Karachi. Letter 2 was written to the editor of 'Express Tribune', Karachi.
questions.explanation: Each letter begins with the date, then 'The Editor', followed by the name of the newspaper and the city. Letter 1 names Daily Dawn and Letter 2 names Express Tribune, both of Karachi.

questions.question: Work in pairs and write a letter to the editor complaining about a problem/issue, following the steps given: brainstorm ideas, select the ideas, decide the name of the newspaper and the gender of the editor, state the problem in paragraph 1, list the reasons in paragraph 2, give suggestions in paragraph 3, use the appropriate format, layout, vocabulary and tone, and edit your work.
questions.answer:
(Model letter to the editor)

15th September, 2024.

The Editor,
Daily Dawn,
Karachi.

Subject: The Growing Menace of Street Crime in Our City

Dear Sir,

Through the columns of your esteemed newspaper, I wish to draw the attention of the concerned authorities to the alarming rise in street crime in our city. Every day we read of mobile phones being snatched, cars and motorcycles being stolen, and houses being robbed in broad daylight. Only last week, a shopkeeper of our area was seriously wounded by robbers who escaped with his day's earnings. Because of this fear, people, especially women and elderly citizens, are afraid to leave their homes after sunset.

The reasons for this lawlessness are not difficult to find. The number of police personnel on patrol is far too small for our fast-growing population, and the police stations are poorly equipped and understaffed. Most of the street and area lights are out of order, which makes the dark lanes a safe playground for criminals. Unemployment, rising inflation and the easy availability of small arms and drugs have pushed many young men towards this path. Above all, careless citizens who keep large amounts of cash and jewellery at home, or who display expensive mobile phones and ornaments in public, make themselves easy targets.

The government must take immediate and effective steps. First, the strength and training of the police should be increased, and patrolling, especially in the evening and at night, should be made more frequent and effective. Second, all street lights must be repaired and new ones installed in the dark areas. Third, honest officials should be rewarded and corrupt or inactive ones punished, so that the common citizen regains confidence in the law-enforcing agencies. Fourth, awareness campaigns should teach people to keep their valuables safely, to cooperate with the police, and to report every incident of crime without delay. Finally, the government should create employment and control inflation so that our youth may turn to honest work instead of crime.

I hope that you will kindly publish this letter and that the authorities concerned will take note of it and act before our city becomes completely unsafe.

Yours faithfully,
A Concerned Citizen
questions.explanation: This model letter follows the standard formal-letter layout: sender's date, address to the editor, a 'Subject' line, an appropriate salutation, three paragraphs (problem, reasons, suggestions) in a polite and serious tone, and a formal closing. It mirrors the two model letters in the textbook.

questions.question: Underline the topic sentence in each body paragraph of the essay 'Deserts'.
questions.answer:
Model response:
Body paragraph 1 - Topic sentence: 'Springs of water are usually few and far apart in deserts.'
Body paragraph 2 - Topic sentence: 'One of the most remarkable deserts in the world is the Sahara Desert.'
Each topic sentence comes at the beginning of its paragraph and announces the key idea that the rest of the paragraph explains with details (springs and oases; the size, surface and oases of the Sahara).
questions.explanation: A topic sentence states the main idea of a body paragraph and is usually placed first, followed by supporting details. The two body paragraphs of 'Deserts' each open with such a sentence.

questions.question: Write a descriptive essay of at least four paragraphs on any one of the following topics: (2) A historical place.
questions.answer:
(Model descriptive essay)
A Historical Place: Mohenjo-Daro

Mohenjo-Daro is one of the oldest and most famous historical places in Pakistan. It lies in the Larkana District of Sindh, on the right bank of the River Indus, and is about 5,000 years old. It was built by the people of the Indus Valley Civilisation and is now a protected site and a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Great numbers of tourists and students visit it every year.

The ruins of Mohenjo-Daro show how advanced its people were. The streets are wide and straight and cross each other at right angles, and the houses are built of baked bricks. The most amazing feature is the covered drain system - each house had a bathroom and its dirty water flowed into the streets' drains. There is also the famous Great Bath, a large tank of bricks where the people perhaps bathed or performed religious rituals, and a tall structure on the highest mound known as the 'Stupa'.

In the museum of Mohenjo-Daro are kept many precious things found during the digging - clay pots, toys, copper and bronze tools, ornaments of gold and silver, and, most wonderful of all, small seals with strange writing that no one has yet been able to read. These objects tell us how the ancient people lived, worked, worshipped and traded with far-off lands.

To conclude, Mohenjo-Daro is not merely a heap of old bricks; it is a mirror in which we see the great skill and discipline of our ancestors. It reminds us that the land of Sindh was once home to one of the greatest civilisations of the ancient world. The government and the people should protect this treasure, for it is the pride of the whole nation.
questions.explanation: A complete four-paragraph descriptive essay on a historical place. It follows the required structure: an introduction ending in a thesis statement, two body paragraphs with topic sentences and vivid details, and a conclusion with a signalling word and a final recommendation.

questions.question: Analyse the two letters to the editor: (b) Are these letters addressed to a man or woman?
questions.answer: Letter 1 is addressed to a man, because it opens with the salutation 'Dear Sir'. Letter 2 is addressed to a woman, because it opens with the salutation 'Dear Madam'.
questions.explanation: The salutation shows the gender of the editor. 'Dear Sir' is used for a man and 'Dear Madam' for a woman. This also shows that the gender of the editor must be considered while writing a formal letter.

questions.question: Discuss how each topic area in the essay 'Deserts' is explained with facts, examples, ideas, opinions, etc.
questions.answer:
Model response:
1. The paragraph on springs and oases explains the topic with an example and details: an oasis is 'an area in the desert where there is water and where plants grow', a place where tired travellers quench their thirst and rest. An opinion is added that without these springs 'no human being could cross the vast stretch of burning sand'.
2. The paragraph on the Sahara supports its topic with facts and figures (it is slightly above sea level, covered with sand, gravels and a mixture of sea shells, and looks like the basin of an evaporated sea) and with numbers (thirty-two springs and oases contain fountains and date palms, twenty of them are inhabited) as well as with the idea that these serve as stopping places for the caravans.
Thus both paragraphs combine facts, examples, descriptions and opinions to develop their key ideas.
questions.explanation: Descriptive writing uses a mixture of facts (numbers, locations), examples (the oasis), descriptions (surface of the Sahara) and opinions to make the topic vivid and convincing.

questions.question: Write a descriptive essay of at least four paragraphs on any one of the following topics: (3) A scenic place.
questions.answer:
(Model descriptive essay)
A Scenic Place: Hunza Valley

Hunza Valley is one of the most beautiful scenic places in Pakistan. It lies in Gilgit-Baltistan, high up in the Karakoram Mountains, along the old Karakoram Highway. Surrounded by snow-covered peaks, deep gorges and green terraces, it is often called 'heaven on earth'. Whoever visits it once can never forget its beauty.

The most striking feature of Hunza is its towering mountains. The valley is watched over by the massive Rakaposhi and the Ultar Peak, whose white peaks shine in the sunlight and turn golden at sunset. Below them flow the icy, rushing waters of the Hunza River, cutting a deep valley through the rocks. On the slopes, apricot, apple, cherry and walnut trees grow in neat rows, and in spring the whole valley is covered with pink and white blossoms.

The people of Hunza are famous for their hospitality, their hard work and their long, healthy lives. The fields are terraced with great skill, and water is carried to them through ancient channels called 'kuls'. Tourists can visit the old Baltit and Altit forts, taste fresh apricots and walnut cake, drink green tea, and buy precious stones and handicrafts. In winter snow covers everything, while in summer the valley is cool and green.

To conclude, Hunza is a place where the mountains, the rivers, the orchards and the people all seem to live together in perfect harmony. Its fresh air, pure water and peaceful beauty refresh both the body and the mind. It is truly one of the loveliest scenic spots in the world, and every Pakistani should visit it at least once.
questions.explanation: A complete four-paragraph descriptive essay on a scenic place. It uses vivid adjectives and adverbs for effect, orders the details from the general view to the finer details, and closes with a signalling phrase and a concluding recommendation.

questions.question: Analyse the two letters to the editor: (c) What problem has been identified in letter 1 and in letter 2?
questions.answer: The problem identified in letter 1 is the very large number of traffic accidents in Pakistan, in which hundreds of people die every year, even though the media and the government focus more on terrorism than on road accidents. The problem identified in letter 2 is the excessive and harmful use of plastic bags, which destroys fertile land, takes more than 500 years to break down in a landfill, and causes deadly diseases such as cancer, birth defects, immune damage and asthma.
questions.explanation: Each letter states its subject in the 'Subject' line and then explains the problem in the first paragraph. Letter 1 is about traffic accidents; letter 2 is about the harm caused by plastic bags.

questions.question: See how the closing paragraph of the essay 'Deserts' is written; underline the signalling closing word or phrase used. Discuss how the paragraph brings together the central idea and all the supporting ideas, and underline the concluding statement - does it give an idea, suggestion or recommendation?
questions.answer: Model response: The closing paragraph begins with the signalling word 'To conclude', which tells the reader that the essay is ending. It brings together the central idea and all the supporting ideas in a short summary: a desert is vast areas of sand with no trees or forests; the only greenery is at the oases where tired and thirsty travellers rest; and travelling in the desert is risky and lack of water can lead to suffering and death. The concluding statement is: 'However, modern technology, including satellite phones and advanced modes of transport, have greatly reduced the risks and sufferings.' This concluding statement gives a suggestion/opinion - that modern technology has made desert travel safer - and so rounds off the essay with a hopeful note.
questions.explanation: A good conclusion uses a signalling word (to conclude, to sum up, in the end), briefly summarises the main points and finishes with a final statement that gives an idea, suggestion or recommendation. 'Deserts' follows exactly this pattern.

questions.question: Write a descriptive essay of at least four paragraphs on any one of the following topics: (4) School playground.
questions.answer:
(Model descriptive essay)
Our School Playground

A school is not complete without a playground, and our school playground is one of its most important places. It is a large open ground at the back of the school building, surrounded on three sides by a low wall and shaded by tall old trees. Although it is a simple place, it is full of life and activity, and it is where students learn as much through games as they do in the classroom.

The playground has different parts for different games. On one side there is a wide cricket pitch with nets, on another a basketball court, and in a corner two volleyball courts. A few swings, a slide and a seesaw stand near the boundary wall for the younger children. Along the walls run long benches where players rest and the Physical Training teacher keeps his whistle, stopwatch and register.

The playground is busiest during the games period and at the interval, when the whole ground seems to come alive with noise and colour. Cricket teams play matches, girls practise basketball, small boys run races, and the air is filled with shouts and laughter. Every year our sports day is held here, when houses compete in races and games and parents come to watch. The playground also teaches us discipline, team spirit and sportsmanship.

To conclude, our school playground is more than a piece of open land; it is a place of health, happiness and friendship. Here we forget our books for a while, build strong bodies and learn to work together. The school should look after it well, for a good playground is the true sign of a lively school.
questions.explanation: A complete four-paragraph descriptive essay on the school playground. It follows the model of 'Deserts' with an introduction ending in a thesis statement, two developed body paragraphs, and a conclusion that uses a signalling phrase and ends with a suggestion.

questions.question: Analyse the two letters to the editor: (d) Which of these letters gives reasons for the problem?
questions.answer: Both letters give reasons for the problem. Letter 1 gives the reasons for traffic accidents: poor conditions of vehicles, violation of traffic rules, use of mobile phones while driving, underage children driving, bad road conditions, and dim or no street lights. Letter 2 gives the reasons (with scientific evidence) for the harm caused by plastic bags: they turn fertile land barren, take more than 500 years to decompose, and are a source of deadly diseases, and their use is increasing by about 15 per cent every year.
questions.explanation: Both letters support their complaint with reasons. Letter 1 lists the causes of road accidents, while letter 2 gives environmental and health reasons supported by scientists and the Ministry of Climate Change.

questions.question: Analyse the two letters to the editor: (e) Which of these letters gives suggestions?
questions.answer: Both letters give suggestions. Letter 1 suggests that the government should take effective steps, such as creating awareness among people through the media and training the traffic police, so that the number of accidents is reduced. Letter 2 suggests that the government should conduct surveys to find out how much damage plastic bags cause, create awareness among people, and pass laws to reduce the use of plastic bags to an essential minimum.
questions.explanation: A good letter to the editor not only states the problem and its reasons but also suggests a solution. Both letters end their body with clear suggestions addressed to the government.

questions.question: Analyse the two letters to the editor: (f) Do we know who wrote both these letters?
questions.answer: No, we do not know both the writers. We know who wrote letter 2, because it is signed by 'Munir Altaf, Turbat'. We do not know the name of the writer of letter 1, because it is signed only as 'A Concerned Citizen, Multan'.
questions.explanation: The signature at the end of a letter reveals the writer's identity. Letter 2 is signed with a full name, whereas letter 1 uses a general description instead of a name.

questions.question: Analyse the two letters to the editor: (g) Why is the name of one writer missing?
questions.answer: The name of one writer is missing because the writer of letter 1 preferred to remain anonymous. Instead of signing his real name, he wrote 'A Concerned Citizen, Multan', which shows that he wanted his message to be read but did not wish to be identified personally. Some writers do this out of modesty or to speak on behalf of the public rather than for themselves.
questions.explanation: Not all letters to the editor are signed with the writer's real name. A signature such as 'A Concerned Citizen' or 'An Angry Reader' is used when the writer wishes to remain anonymous.

questions.question: Editing: Work in pairs and read the story 'The Wise King'. It contains many types of errors - grammatical, punctuation, capitalization and spelling. Correct all the underlined errors, first orally and then rewrite the corrected story in your notebooks.
questions.answer:
(Corrected story)

The Wise King

A rich man was on his death bed. He told his sons to dig the ground under his cot and share the buried wealth. After his death, when he died, the sons started digging. One of them found a vessel full of jewels and pearls, another a vessel full of gold and silver coins, the third one a vessel full of bones, and the first a vessel full of dust. The last two quarrelled with the first three and said that the riches should be shared equally among them. The first two did not agree.

Finally, all four decided to put their case before the king. The king listened to their story and decided that the one who got the jewels should keep them and the one who got the coins should also keep them. The other two brothers felt very sad when they heard this.

Then the king looked at the other two brothers and said that the one who had the vessel full of bones was to be the owner of the cattle left by their father, and the one with the vessel that had dust was to get all the land owned by the rich man. This decision by the king pleased all the brothers. They were amazed at the king's wisdom. They were all satisfied and happy with the decision.
questions.explanation: Corrections made: 'her sons' -> 'his sons'; 'when he die' -> 'when he died'; 'sons starts' -> 'sons started'; 'one of them find' -> 'one of them found'; 'pards' -> 'pearls'; the question mark after 'them' -> a full stop and a capital 'The'; 'the on who' -> 'the one who'; 'should kept' -> 'should keep'; 'the one whose' -> 'the one who'; 'very said' -> 'very sad'; 'when the heard' -> 'when they heard'; 'two daughters' -> 'two brothers'; 'by her father' -> 'by their father'; 'that has dust' -> 'that had dust'; 'the minister' -> 'the king'; 'was liked all the brothers' -> 'pleased all the brothers'; 'They amazed' -> 'They were amazed'; 'the kings' -> 'the king's'; 'They was' -> 'They were'.

questions.question: Editing: The story 'The Four Seasons' has about twenty errors. Read the story, underline the errors, write the correct form above them, and then write the corrected story in your notebooks.
questions.answer:
(Corrected story)

The Four Seasons

There was a man who had four sons. He wanted his sons to learn not to judge things too quickly. So he sent each one of them, one by one, to go and look at a pear tree that was a great distance away.

The first son went in winter, the second in spring, the third in summer and the youngest son in autumn. When they had all gone and come back, he called them together to describe what they had seen. The first son said that the tree was ugly, bent and twisted. The second son said, 'No, it was covered with green buds and full of promise.' The third son disagreed; he said it was laden with blossoms that smelled so sweet and looked so beautiful; it was the most graceful thing he had ever seen. The last son disagreed with all of them; he said it was drooping with ripe fruit, full of life and fulfilment.

The man then explained to his sons that they were all right, because they had each seen but only one season in the tree's life. He told them that you cannot judge a tree, or a person, by only one season, or on the basis of knowing about only one aspect of his life. So, don't let the pain of one season destroy the joy of all the rest. Don't judge life by one difficult season, or people on the basis of one bad example.
questions.explanation: Corrections made: 'four son' -> 'four sons'; 'he wanted' -> 'He wanted' and the run-on comma -> a full stop; 'to learnt' -> 'to learn'; 'So he send' -> 'So he sent'; 'them each one of them' -> 'each one of them'; 'look at pear tree' -> 'look at a pear tree'; 'the second on spring' -> 'the second in spring'; 'the youngest son' -> 'the youngest son' (kept) ; 'had all go and come back' -> 'had all gone and come back'; 'had see' -> 'had seen'; 'twisted the second son said no if was' -> 'twisted. The second son said, No, it was'; 'The three son' -> 'The third son'; 'look so beautiful' -> 'looked so beautiful'; 'it was most graceful' -> 'it was the most graceful'; 'disagreed all of them' -> 'disagreed with all of them'; 'dropping with ripe fruit' -> 'drooping with ripe fruit'; 'his son' -> 'his sons'; 'in the trees life' -> 'in the tree's life'; 'He tell them' -> 'He told them'; 'Dont' -> 'Don't'. About twenty corrections in all, matching the teacher's note (five in the first and third paragraphs and ten in the second).

questions.question: Travel brochure (Step 1): Think of a place that you want people to visit and brainstorm for ideas about why people should visit that place, what they need to take with them, the modes of travel, the things they must see, eat and buy, and important things to remember.
questions.answer:
Model brainstorm for a brochure about Hunza Valley:
Why people should visit: breathtaking snow-covered mountains (Rakaposhi, Ultar Peak), the crystal-clear Hunza River, terraced orchards, ancient forts (Baltit and Altit), warm and hospitable people, and the healthiest and longest-living people of Pakistan.
What to take: warm clothes, walking shoes, sunglasses and sun-block, a first-aid box, a camera, cash (as ATM facilities are limited), and any personal medicines.
Modes of travel: by air to Gilgit, or by road along the Karakoram Highway in a car, bus or coaster; within the valley, by jeep or on foot.
Things to see: Rakaposhi View Point, Attabad Lake, the Baltit and Altit Forts, the Duikar sunrise point, the Pakistan-China border at Khunjerab Pass.
Things to eat: apricots and apricot soup, walnut cake, chapshuro, fresh cherries, mulberry jam, and local green tea (Hunza tea).
Things to buy: gemstones and precious stones, woollen shawls, hand-made caps, dried fruits and apricot oil.
Things to remember: keep the valley clean and do not litter, respect local customs and dress modestly, take photographs only with permission, and do not pluck fruit without the owner's consent.
questions.explanation: This is the brainstorming step of the travel-brochure activity. The points answer each of the sub-questions in Step 1 and give the group ready material for a colourful, informative brochure.

questions.question: Travel brochure (Step 2): Discuss and decide a name for your travel agency, think about what your brochure will look like (shape, writing, pictures or drawings), decide who will do what, and start developing the brochure.
questions.answer:
Model plan:
Name of the travel agency: 'Roof of the World Travels' (other choices: 'Peak Adventures', 'Silk Route Tours', 'Hunza Horizons').
Look of the brochure: a three-fold (tri-fold) coloured pamphlet on art paper, about 21 cm x 30 cm; cover page with a big photograph of Rakaposhi and the agency's name in bold letters; inside, three panels - 'Why Visit Hunza?', 'What to See and Do', and 'Travel Tips and Contacts'; each panel has a short heading, two or three sentences of brief information, a small map of the valley, and colourful pictures or hand-made drawings of mountains, apricots and forts; the back page gives the agency's phone number, e-mail and a warm closing line such as 'Come and see the roof of the world!'
Division of work: one member collects facts and pictures from the internet, the tourism office or a travel agent; one writes the text; one draws and arranges the pictures and designs the cover; one checks the spelling, punctuation and final layout.
Presentation: the finished brochure is displayed in the classroom or school, and the group explains its brochure to the class.
questions.explanation: This is the planning and production step of the Fun activity. The brochure should be colourful but brief, giving short, clear information about the chosen place, as the textbook explains that a brochure is a kind of pamphlet giving brief information about a programme, place or activity.

questions.question: Who is your favourite poet?
questions.answer: My favourite poet is Allama Muhammad Iqbal, because his poetry awakens a sense of hope, self-respect and love for one's homeland. I also admire Shah Abdul Latif Bhitai, whose verses carry a message of love and devotion. Discussing my choice with my partner helped me learn why different people admire different poets.
questions.explanation: This is the first pre-reading discussion question; it is meant to be answered orally in pairs before reading the text about Shah Abdul Latif.

questions.question: How many aspects of Shah Abdul Latif's life have been covered in the text?
questions.answer: Seven aspects of Shah Abdul Latif's life have been covered in the text.
questions.explanation: The reading text is divided into seven numbered sections, each dealing with one aspect of the poet's life: Background and Family, The Name Bhitai, Early Life and Education, Youth, Spiritual Growth, Death and Remembrance, and Shah Latif's Poetry.

questions.question: Those who have an abundance of wealth have ______.
questions.answer: Those who have an abundance of wealth have a lot of wealth.
questions.explanation: 'Abundance' means a very large quantity of something, so having an abundance of wealth means having a lot of wealth.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) little wealth (b) a lot of wealth (c) some wealth

questions.question: The ______ of Shah Bhitai celebrate his Urs every year.
questions.answer: The devotees of Shah Bhitai celebrate his Urs every year.
questions.explanation: The bold words of Exercise 2 are to be used once each; a devotee is a devoted follower, so 'devotees' fits here.

questions.question: He found pleasure in praying, thinking and devotion. (Write the aspect number.)
questions.answer: 5 (Spiritual Growth).
questions.explanation: The section on Spiritual Growth says that Latif's love of God grew so much that he found pleasure only in devotion and spent most of his time in prayers and deep thinking.

questions.question: Two things done at the time of 'Urs', as mentioned in the text.
questions.answer: At the time of the Urs, (i) thousands of people gather and listen to the saint's songs sung on the Tambooro, and (ii) many learned men read papers that tell about Latif's life and his poetry.
questions.explanation: The Urs is held at his shrine every year on 14th Safar, the second month of the Muslim calendar, and lasts for three days.

questions.question: How was information about Shah Latif's early life collected? Why was it collected in this manner?
questions.answer: Information about Shah Latif's early life was mostly collected from oral traditions. The renowned Pakistani scholar, educationist and writer Mirza Kalich Beg collected details about his early life from some of the old people living at that time. These people had heard the facts from their fathers and grandfathers, some of whom had seen Shah Latif in person and had even spoken to him. It was collected in this manner because no written records of his early life existed, so the only available source was the memory and word-of-mouth accounts of people who had lived near him.
questions.explanation: This question tests inference: the text is written on the basis of oral traditions, and the reason is the absence of contemporary written records.

questions.question: Work in groups of six and prepare questions for conducting an interview of scholars who have studied Shah Abdul Latif Bhitai, his life and his poetry. Then prepare a role play in which one member becomes an anchor person while the remaining members become scholars in a TV talk show.
questions.answer: Model interview questions for the TV talk show (the anchor asks each of the five 'scholars' two questions): 1. When and where was Shah Abdul Latif Bhitai born, and what was his family background? 2. Why did his ancestors migrate from Afghanistan to Sindh? 3. Why is he called 'Bhitai' or the 'Saint of Bhit'? 4. What kind of education did he receive, and which languages did he know? 5. Tell us about his married life and why he never married again. 6. How did he spend his time at the mound and by the lake? 7. What is Shah Jo Risalo, and why is it so important in Sindhi literature? 8. Which distant places and which Sindhi sailors are mentioned in his poetry? 9. What is the main message of his poetry, and why is it acceptable to people of every faith? 10. How is his Urs celebrated every year at his shrine? Role play outline: One student acts as the anchor and opens the show by welcoming the audience and introducing the topic 'Shah Abdul Latif Bhitai: The Role Model of Sindh'. The anchor then asks two questions to each of the five panellists in turn; each panellist answers briefly in a respectful, scholarly tone, using facts from the reading text. The anchor closes the show by thanking the scholars and summarising Shah Latif's message of love.
questions.explanation: This is a group activity in which students prepare ten questions and perform a TV talk show role play; the model above supplies the questions and the structure of the role play.

questions.question: Share some couplets that you like.
questions.answer: I like the following couplet by Allama Iqbal: 'Khudi ko kar buland itna ke har taqdeer se pehle, Khuda bande se khud poochhe, bata teri raza kya hai' ('Raise yourself so high that before every decree, God Himself asks you, tell Me, what is your wish'). I also like Shah Latif's verse in which he prays, 'My beloved Allah, may you always make Sindh, a land of abundance.' These couplets teach hope, self-belief and love for one's land.
questions.explanation: A pre-reading oral activity that encourages students to recall and share poetry they already know.

questions.question: List all these aspects in your notebook as shown below. (The first aspect is about his Background and Family.)
questions.answer: The first aspect is about his Background and Family. The second aspect is about The Name Bhitai. The third aspect is about his Early Life and Education. The fourth aspect is about his Youth. The fifth aspect is about his Spiritual Growth. The sixth aspect is about his Death and Remembrance. The seventh aspect is about Shah Latif's Poetry.
questions.explanation: Students must list, in order, the seven headings used to organise the reading text on Shah Abdul Latif Bhitai.

questions.question: My family's ancestral roots are in Sindh, means my parents, grandparents and great grandparents have lived in Sindh since ______.
questions.answer: My family's ancestral roots are in Sindh, means my parents, grandparents and great grandparents have lived in Sindh since many generations.
questions.explanation: 'Ancestral roots' refers to the place from which one's family originally came and where it has lived for many generations.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) my grandparents got married (b) my birth (c) many generations

questions.question: My mother and I decided to go to a ______ to ask him to pray for my father's health.
questions.answer: My mother and I decided to go to a mystic to ask him to pray for my father's health.
questions.explanation: A mystic is a person with spiritual power to whom people go for prayers and blessings.

questions.question: He was married for a short period of time only. (Write the aspect number.)
questions.answer: 4 (Youth).
questions.explanation: The section on Youth tells us that Shah Latif married Bibi Saidha Begum in 1713 and his wife died at an early age, so the marriage lasted only a short time.

questions.question: Two possible reasons why his ancestors migrated to Sindh.
questions.answer: (i) Shah's father, Syed Habib Shah, migrated from Matyaru in Afghanistan to Bhainpur in Sindh in order to gain spiritual contact with Bilawal, a local pious man; (ii) Sindh was then a centre of Muslim culture and Shah Latif's ancestors liked it so much that they decided to make it their home.
questions.explanation: Some historians give the reason of spiritual contact with Bilawal, while others say that his ancestors migrated to Sindh from Hirat and stayed because they liked the land.

questions.question: Why is Shah Latif called the 'Saint of Bhit'?
questions.answer: Shah Latif is called the 'Saint of Bhit' because in 1742 he left his home and went to live on a mound at some distance from his village. A mound of sand is called 'bhit' in Sindhi, and since he lived on this mound for the rest of his life, he came to be known as the Saint of Bhit, Shah Abdul Latif Bhitai, or Shah Latif of the Mound.
