Model sentences using two synonyms from each of six groups of Exercise 3:

Group (a) - friendly / amicable:
1. Our new neighbour is very friendly and always greets us with a smile.
2. After a long argument, the two brothers reached an amicable settlement.

Group (b) - choice / alternative:
3. You must make your own choice about the subjects you wish to study in Class X.
4. Solar power is an excellent alternative to electricity produced from coal.

Group (d) - severe / stern:
5. The severe heat of June made it very difficult to work outdoors.
6. Our coach gave us a stern look when we arrived late for practice.

Group (e) - huge / enormous:
7. A huge crowd had gathered at the stadium to watch the final match.
8. The blue whale is an enormous creature of the sea.

Group (g) - intelligent / clever:
9. Sara is an intelligent student who answers every question thoughtfully.
10. It was a clever plan that saved our team from defeat.

Group (j) - illness / ailment:
11. He stayed at home for a whole week because of a serious illness.
12. Old age often brings minor ailments such as joint pain and poor eyesight.
questions.explanation: This exercise makes the students use synonyms actively rather than only recognising them. Writing the two words in different sentences shows that although they are similar in meaning they are not always interchangeable in a given context.

questions.question: Exercise 5 blank 1: My father is a remarkable man. He has been working ______ he was 15 years old.
questions.answer: My father is a remarkable man. He has been working since he was 15 years old.
questions.explanation: 'Since' is used with a point of time in the past (when he was 15) from which an action has continued up to now, and with the present perfect continuous tense.

questions.question: Exercise 6: Write a paragraph explaining what your three favourite hobbies or free time activities are or were. Explain why you started, how long you have done them for, when you started them, do you still do them, and why you like them so much. Remember to use 'for' and 'since' in your sentences.
questions.answer:
Model paragraph:

One thing I like doing during my free time is reading. I have been reading story books since I was ten years old, when my elder sister gave me a collection of folk tales and I fell in love with stories at once. So I have been reading story books for nearly six years now. Although I have been reading since I was ten, I think I will do it for many more years; in fact, I think I will do it for the rest of my life. Another thing I enjoy is playing cricket with my friends in the street. I started playing it when I was in Class VI, because our physical training teacher told us that games keep the body healthy and the mind fresh. I have been playing cricket for about three years now, and I still play every evening whenever my school work is finished. Yet another thing that I did for a long time was gardening with my grandfather. I began helping him in our small garden when I was eight, and we worked together for almost four years. Sadly, my grandfather passed away two years ago and we moved to a flat, so I have not done any gardening since then; but I still love plants, and I hope to start a small garden of my own one day.
questions.explanation: The exercise practises 'for' (with a duration - for three years, for the rest of my life) and 'since' (with a starting point - since I was ten, since then). The model paragraph answers all the questions asked: what, why, how long, when, whether it continues, and why the writer likes the activity.

questions.question: Exercise 1 Q2: Rewrite the sentence by replacing the bold synonym 'difficult' with an appropriate synonym from the options: Mrs Amjad gave the class a difficult assignment for chemistry.
questions.answer: Mrs Amjad gave the class a hard assignment for chemistry.
questions.explanation: 'Difficult' means not easy to do, and 'hard' is its direct synonym. 'Free', 'easy' and 'caring' have quite different meanings.

questions.question: Exercise 2 (b): Select the most appropriate synonym to complete the sentence: If one wants to succeed in the exams, it is ______ to study regularly (primary, important, significant).
questions.answer: If one wants to succeed in the exams, it is important to study regularly.
questions.explanation: 'Important' is the natural word for something necessary to achieve a result. 'Primary' means first in order, and 'significant' means notable, so neither fits this sentence as well.

questions.question: Exercise 3 (b): Four of the following five words are synonyms; circle the word that is different: option, nice, choice, possibility, alternative.
questions.answer: The different word is 'nice'. The other four - option, choice, possibility and alternative - all mean something that may be chosen or may happen.
questions.explanation: 'Nice' means pleasant or agreeable and has nothing to do with choosing, so it is the odd word out.

questions.question: Exercise 5 blank 2: He has been working ______ he was at school.
questions.answer: He has been working since he was at school.
questions.explanation: Here 'he was at school' is a point of time in the past, so 'since' is needed, not 'for', which would require a period of time.

questions.question: Exercise 1 Q3: Rewrite the sentence by replacing the bold synonym 'old' with an appropriate synonym from the options: My grandmother is old. She is about 90 years old.
questions.answer: My grandmother is elderly. She is about 90 years old.
questions.explanation: 'Elderly' is the polite synonym for 'old' when speaking of a person's age. 'Crazy', 'charming' and 'friendly' describe character, not age.

questions.question: Exercise 2 (c): Select the most appropriate synonym to complete the sentence: During the monsoon rains the water in the rivers becomes very ______ (disordered, violent, rough).
questions.answer: During the monsoon rains the water in the rivers becomes very rough.
questions.explanation: 'Rough' is the word used for disturbed, uneven water. 'Violent' is used for people or acts of force, and 'disordered' is used for things that are not arranged properly.

questions.question: Exercise 3 (c): Four of the following five words are synonyms; circle the word that is different: reasonable, rude, impolite, cheeky, disrespectful.
questions.answer: The different word is 'reasonable'. The other four - rude, impolite, cheeky and disrespectful - all describe bad manners.
questions.explanation: 'Reasonable' means sensible and fair, which is the opposite of the rudeness shown by the other four words.

questions.question: Exercise 5 blank 3: He used to work ______ four hours every day and on weekends.
questions.answer: He used to work for four hours every day and on weekends.
questions.explanation: 'Four hours' is a period or duration of time, and 'for' is used with periods of time in any tense.

questions.question: Exercise 1 Q4: Rewrite the sentence by replacing the bold synonym 'slim' with an appropriate synonym from the options: Our principal is very smart and slim.
questions.answer: Our principal is very smart and thin.
questions.explanation: 'Slim' means thin in an attractive way, so 'thin' is the closest synonym here. 'Tall', 'charming' and 'strict' do not mean slim.

questions.question: Exercise 2 (d): Select the most appropriate synonym to complete the sentence: The ruins of Moen-jo-Daro are ______ (old, past, aged).
questions.answer: The ruins of Moen-jo-Daro are old.
questions.explanation: 'Old' is the correct word for things that have existed for a long time. 'Past' means gone by in time, and 'aged' is generally used for people or things that have grown grey with years.

questions.question: Exercise 3 (d): Four of the following five words are synonyms; circle the word that is different: severe, serious, harsh, stable, stern.
questions.answer: The different word is 'stable'. The other four - severe, serious, harsh and stern - all mean strict or harsh in nature.
questions.explanation: 'Stable' means firm and not likely to change, which is a different idea from the strictness expressed by the other four words.

questions.question: Exercise 5 blank 4: He has now worked in the same factory ______ 25 years.
questions.answer: He has now worked in the same factory for 25 years.
questions.explanation: '25 years' is the length or duration of the period, so 'for' is used even with the present perfect tense.

questions.question: Exercise 1 Q5: Rewrite the sentence by replacing the bold synonym 'stable' with an appropriate synonym from the options: A stable government ensures that a nation will progress.
questions.answer: A steady government ensures that a nation will progress.
questions.explanation: 'Stable' means firm and not likely to change, so 'steady' is the best synonym. 'Friendly', 'strong' and 'outgoing' do not carry the idea of firmness and continuity.

questions.question: Exercise 2 (e): Select the most appropriate synonym to complete the sentence: Pakistan is ______ in minerals (rich, wealthy, affluent).
questions.answer: Pakistan is rich in minerals.
questions.explanation: 'Rich in' is the fixed expression used for countries that have plenty of a natural resource. 'Wealthy' and 'affluent' are used for people who have a lot of money.

questions.question: Exercise 3 (e): Four of the following five words are synonyms; circle the word that is different: huge, large, enormous, mammoth, many.
questions.answer: The different word is 'many'. The other four - huge, large, enormous and mammoth - all mean very big in size.
questions.explanation: 'Many' tells us the number of things, not their size, so it does not belong with the other four words.

questions.question: Exercise 5 blank 5: ______ he started working at the factory, he has been promoted many times.
questions.answer: Since he started working at the factory, he has been promoted many times.
questions.explanation: 'Since' introduces the starting point of an action that continues up to the present; it is placed at the beginning of the clause here and is written with a capital letter.

questions.question: Exercise 1 Q6: Rewrite the sentence by replacing the bold synonym 'help' with an appropriate synonym from the options: Farzana is always ready to help the people in her neighbourhood.
questions.answer: Farzana is always ready to assist the people in her neighbourhood.
questions.explanation: 'Assist' is the formal synonym of 'help'. 'Teach', 'guide' and 'train' mean something more specific than helping.

questions.question: Exercise 2 (f): Select the most appropriate synonym to complete the sentence: My mother has to go to the NADRA office because her ID card is no longer ______ (valid, authorized, legitimate).
questions.answer: My mother has to go to the NADRA office because her ID card is no longer valid.
questions.explanation: 'Valid' means legally usable and still in force, which is exactly the meaning needed for a document such as an identity card.

questions.question: Exercise 3 (f): Four of the following five words are synonyms; circle the word that is different: rubbish, garbage, garden, trash, refuse.
questions.answer: The different word is 'garden'. The other four - rubbish, garbage, trash and refuse - all mean waste material that is thrown away.
questions.explanation: A garden is a piece of ground where flowers and vegetables are grown, so it has nothing to do with waste.

questions.question: Exercise 5 blank 6: He was initially hired ______ a period of three months.
questions.answer: He was initially hired for a period of three months.
questions.explanation: 'A period of three months' is a duration, so 'for' is the correct preposition.

questions.question: Exercise 1 Q7: Rewrite the sentence by replacing the bold synonym 'drowsy' with an appropriate synonym from the options: I feel drowsy after having rice for lunch.
questions.answer: I feel sleepy after having rice for lunch.
questions.explanation: 'Drowsy' means half asleep, so 'sleepy' is its exact synonym. 'Lazy', 'active' and 'happy' do not mean drowsy.

questions.question: Exercise 2 (g): Select the most appropriate synonym to complete the sentence: The bangles her grandmother gave her are made of ______ gold (true, correct, real).
questions.answer: The bangles her grandmother gave her are made of real gold.
questions.explanation: 'Real' means genuine, not imitation, so it is the right word for pure gold. 'True' means correct or faithful, and 'correct' means free from error; neither is used for metals.

questions.question: Exercise 3 (g): Four of the following five words are synonyms; circle the word that is different: polite, intelligent, smart, clever, bright.
questions.answer: The different word is 'polite'. The other four - intelligent, smart, clever and bright - all describe a person who has a quick and able mind.
questions.explanation: 'Polite' describes good manners, not intelligence, so it is the odd word in this group.

questions.question: Exercise 5 blank 7: But he has been working there ever ______.
questions.answer: But he has been working there ever since.
questions.explanation: 'Ever since' is a fixed expression meaning continuously from the time mentioned (the end of those first three months) up to now.

questions.question: Exercise 1 Q8: Rewrite the sentence by replacing the bold synonym 'vacant' with an appropriate synonym from the options: The house next door has been vacant for two years.
questions.answer: The house next door has been empty for two years.
questions.explanation: 'Vacant' means not occupied or empty, so 'empty' is the correct synonym. 'Dirty', 'robbed' and 'painted' do not give the meaning of vacancy.

questions.question: Exercise 2 (h): Select the most appropriate synonym to complete the sentence: The teacher asked the students to remain ______ as the class next door was doing a test (still, quiet, noiseless).
questions.answer: The teacher asked the students to remain quiet as the class next door was doing a test.
questions.explanation: 'Quiet' means making little or no noise and is used for people. 'Still' means without movement, and 'noiseless' is generally used for machines or actions, not for people who must keep silent.

questions.question: Exercise 3 (h): Four of the following five words are synonyms; circle the word that is different: position, vacancy, opening, clean, post.
questions.answer: The different word is 'clean'. The other four - position, vacancy, opening and post - all mean a job that is available.
questions.explanation: 'Clean' means free from dirt and is an adjective, whereas the other four words are nouns meaning a place of work or an available job.

questions.question: Exercise 5 blank 8: He started working ______ Rs 25/- a day.
questions.answer: He started working for Rs 25/- a day.
questions.explanation: Here 'for' means 'in exchange for' or 'at a wage of', which is the fixed usage with wages and rates of pay.

questions.question: Exercise 2 (i): Select the most appropriate synonym to complete the sentence: This perfume has a lovely ______ (odour, smell, fragrance).
questions.answer: This perfume has a lovely fragrance.
questions.explanation: 'Fragrance' is the pleasant, sweet smell of a perfume. 'Odour' is often used for an unpleasant smell, and 'smell' is a neutral word.

questions.question: Exercise 3 (i): Four of the following five words are synonyms; circle the word that is different: mistake, correct, error, inaccuracy, slip.
questions.answer: The different word is 'correct'. The other four - mistake, error, inaccuracy and slip - all mean something that is wrong.
questions.explanation: 'Correct' means free from error, which is the opposite of the other four words; it is therefore the odd word out.

questions.question: Exercise 5 blank 9: If he fell ill or if he was absent he did not get paid ______ that day.
questions.answer: If he fell ill or if he was absent he did not get paid for that day.
questions.explanation: 'For that day' means in respect of that particular day; 'for' is used with a period of time even when it is as short as one day.

questions.question: Exercise 2 (j): Select the most appropriate synonym to complete the sentence: The entire staff in the office was full of ______ for the new manager (appreciation, admiration, praise).
questions.answer: The entire staff in the office was full of admiration for the new manager.
questions.explanation: 'Full of admiration for' is the natural collocation, meaning a feeling of great respect and liking. 'Appreciation' and 'praise' are things that are expressed, not feelings one is 'full of'.

questions.question: Exercise 3 (j): Four of the following five words are synonyms; circle the word that is different: disease, ailment, wound, illness, disorder.
questions.answer: The different word is 'wound'. The other four - disease, ailment, illness and disorder - all mean a sickness or a bad condition of health.
questions.explanation: A wound is an injury to the body caused by a cut, blow or weapon, not an illness, so it is the odd word in this group.

questions.question: Exercise 5 blank 10: He only took off ______ serious emergencies, like illness and death.
questions.answer: He only took off for serious emergencies, like illness and death.
questions.explanation: 'To take off for something' means to stay away from work because of that reason, so 'for' is used here to show the purpose or cause.

questions.question: Exercise 5 blank 11: In fact, there were periods when he didn't take a single holiday ______ many months at a time.
questions.answer: In fact, there were periods when he didn't take a single holiday for many months at a time.
questions.explanation: 'Many months at a time' is a duration, so 'for' is the correct preposition.

questions.question: Exercise 5 blank 12: He soon earned the respect of his co-workers and boss, and ______ then, he has risen higher and higher.
questions.answer: He soon earned the respect of his co-workers and boss, and since then, he has risen higher and higher.
questions.explanation: 'Since then' marks the point of time (that time) from which his rise has continued up to the present, and it goes with the present perfect tense.

questions.question: Exercise 5 blank 13: He has now worked for the same factory ______ 25 years.
questions.answer: He has now worked for the same factory for 25 years.
questions.explanation: '25 years' is the duration of the period of work, so 'for' is required. (The sentence uses 'for the same factory' in the sense of 'worked in the same factory'.)

questions.question: Exercise 5 blank 14: He was offered retirement when he completed 25 years, but he said that he would like to work ______ a few more years.
questions.answer: He was offered retirement when he completed 25 years, but he said that he would like to work for a few more years.
questions.explanation: 'A few more years' is a period of time, so 'for' is the correct preposition. Here 'would like to work for' also means to work in exchange for those years.

questions.question: Exercise 1 (Narrative Essay - Further Practice): Imagine you are reporters for a newspaper. An important event has taken place in your area and you have to write a report and submit it for publication. Work in groups of three, share one important event or incident each, choose one of the stories and, following the steps given in Unit 2.4 Exercise 3, write a narrative essay of at least four paragraphs about it.
questions.answer:
Model narrative report (newspaper style):

A Free Medical Camp Brings Relief to the People of Our Town

By: A Student Reporter, Class IX

Our town, which has more than twenty thousand residents, has only one government dispensary and no proper hospital. For years the poor people of our area had to travel forty kilometres to the city even for a small check-up. Last Sunday, however, an important event took place that brought great relief to hundreds of families: a free medical camp was set up in the Government Boys' School ground by a group of volunteer doctors and the students of our school.

The camp began at eight o'clock in the morning and continued until sunset. Ten doctors and nurses, most of them from the city's teaching hospital, examined the patients free of charge, and medicines were also given free of cost. The volunteers had arranged four separate sections - one for children, one for women, one for eye patients and one for general check-ups. In the afternoon a short talk on cleanliness and the prevention of dengue fever was also given to the waiting crowd. I myself helped at the registration desk, where more than six hundred patients were registered during the day.

The event had been organised after a sad incident that had shaken our town only a month earlier. A nine-year-old boy of our neighbourhood, the son of a poor cart-puller, had died of typhoid because his father could not afford to take him to the city for treatment. His death made the students of our school realise that good health is the right of every human being and not a luxury of the rich. The students collected donations, the local traders gave medicines, and the school management allowed the use of the ground. The camp cost almost nothing to the poor patients because everybody contributed according to his ability.

The significance of this event is very great, both for my town and for me personally. For the town it means that hundreds of people received treatment and advice who would otherwise have remained ill, and it has taught our people that we can solve our own problems by working together. For me personally, it was a lesson in service and social responsibility. I learnt that a report is not merely a description of an event; it is a record of what a community can achieve when its members join hands.
questions.explanation: A narrative report tells when and where the event took place, what happened with significant details, and why it matters at the personal, social and national levels. This model follows the structure taught in Unit 2.4 - introduction setting the scene, the event itself, the circumstances that led to it, and a concluding paragraph on its importance.

questions.question: Exercise 2 (Summary Writing): Work in pairs. Read the passage 'Helen Keller' and underline the main ideas/words in each paragraph; do not include any details. The first paragraph has been done as an example.
questions.answer:
Main ideas/key words of each paragraph of the passage 'Helen Keller':

Paragraph 1 (the example): Most people are lucky to be able to see and hear, but some people are blind and deaf; those who lost their sight and hearing after once having them are the most unfortunate; many such people are brave and courageous - and one of them was Helen Keller.

Paragraph 2: Helen Keller was born in 1880 in a small town in the United States of America; she was a normal child up to the age of two; in February 1882 she fell seriously ill and became blind and deaf; her parents were sad but never lost hope.

Paragraph 3: When Helen was seven her life changed completely; her father heard about Miss Sullivan, a woman who had once been blind but had regained her sight and who now helped blind people; her father asked Miss Sullivan to come and teach Helen, and she agreed.

Paragraph 4: One day at the river bank Miss Sullivan taught Helen to spell 'water' by dipping her hand in the water; Helen felt excited because there was now some light in her dark world; kindly and patiently Miss Sullivan went on to teach her about mountains, rivers, history, geography, counting and sums.

Paragraph 5: When Helen was eight she was sent to a school for blind children; although she could speak she had forgotten how, so her teacher helped her to regain her speech by making her feel the movements of her lips; after many exercises, at the age of ten, she was able to speak again.

Paragraph 6: By and by Helen learnt to read books printed in Braille by touching the raised points with her fingers; she read as much as other people, passed all her examinations easily, went to college and then to Harvard University, and graduated without difficulty, proving to be a better student than many others.

Paragraph 7: In 1956, at seventy-six, Helen Keller visited Pakistan to see how she could help other deaf and blind people; she addressed many gatherings and encouraged those with similar shortcomings, visited the school for the deaf, dumb and blind in Karachi, told the students to be happy and cheerful and never to curse their fate, and praised the volunteers for their zeal and self-less dedication.
questions.explanation: Underlining the main ideas and key words of each paragraph, and leaving out details, is the first step of summary writing. The seven main ideas listed here are the skeleton from which the summary in Exercise 3 is written.

questions.question: Exercise 3: Work in pairs. Use the underlined key words and write a summary of the passage 'Helen Keller'. Look at the Do's and Don'ts given in the boxes in Unit 2.4. You may begin like this: 'Most people are very lucky as they can see all things around them. But some people cannot see or hear...'
questions.answer:
Summary of the passage 'Helen Keller':

Most people are very lucky as they can see all things around them. But some people cannot see or hear. However, there are also those unfortunate ones who could once see and hear but are now blind and deaf. Some such people are brave and they take this as a challenge. One such person was Helen Keller. She was born in America in 1880 and was a normal child up to the age of two, but in February 1882 she fell seriously ill and became blind and deaf. Her parents were sad, yet they never lost hope. When Helen was seven, her life changed completely, because Miss Sullivan, a woman who had once been blind but had regained her sight, came to teach her. Miss Sullivan first taught her the word 'water' by dipping her hand in the river, and then patiently taught her about mountains and rivers, history and geography, counting and sums. When Helen was eight she was sent to a school for blind children, where her teacher helped her to regain her lost speech by letting her feel the movements of her lips; by the age of ten she could speak again. She learnt to read books printed in Braille by touching the raised points with her fingers, passed all her examinations easily, went to college and then to Harvard University, and graduated without difficulty. In 1956, although she was seventy-six, she visited Pakistan to help the deaf and blind. She encouraged them to be happy and cheerful and told them that they could do everything in this world.
questions.explanation: A good summary keeps only the main ideas, follows the order of the original, uses the writer's own words where possible, does not repeat details or examples, and gives the whole passage in about one-fourth of its length. This model of about 250 words fits all these rules.

questions.question: Exercise 1: Work in pairs. Read the information about K2 given in the table and write an essay about K2 by following these steps: (1) Discuss in how many paragraphs you can divide the given information. (2) Write an introductory paragraph about Pakistan, its physical features and the high mountains of Northern Pakistan, ending with a sentence stating what you will write about K2. (3) Write a good topic sentence for each paragraph. (4) Write the supporting details for each topic sentence (3-5 sentences). (5) Write a concluding paragraph. (6) Edit for spelling, punctuation and grammar. (7) Exchange your essay with another pair and give feedback. (8) Revise and write it in your notebooks.
questions.answer:
Plan: The information in the table divides naturally into five paragraphs - (i) introduction on Pakistan and its mountains, (ii) location, height and range of K2, (iii) the names and nicknames of K2, (iv) the history of its climbing, and (v) Pakistani climbers, danger and conclusion.

K2: The Savage Mountain of Pakistan

Pakistan is a land of striking physical beauty. It has high mountains, green valleys, glaciers, rivers, lakes and deserts, and among all these features the mountains of the north are the most impressive. These areas are the meeting place of the three greatest mountain ranges in the world - the Himalayas, the Karakoram and the Hindu Kush - and they contain some of the highest peaks on the earth. This essay describes one of those peaks, K2, the mightiest mountain of Pakistan.

K2 is the second-highest mountain in the world and the highest mountain of Pakistan. It stands on the Pakistan-China border, between Gilgit in Gilgit-Baltistan and the Tashkurgan Tajik Autonomous County of Xinjiang in China, and it forms part of the Karakoram range. Its height is 28,253 feet, that is 8,612 metres, which makes it the second-highest peak in the world after Mount Everest and the highest peak within Pakistan.

The mountain has several names. The name 'K2' was given in 1852 by the British surveyor T. G. Montgomerie: 'K' stands for the Karakoram range and '2' for the second-highest peak. It was later named Mount Godwin-Austen after Haversham Godwin-Austen, a British surveyor and explorer. The local Balti people call it Chogori, meaning 'large mountain'; in Chinese it is Qogir, meaning 'Great Mountain'; and another local name is Kechu. Because of its terrible weather and high death rate it is nicknamed the 'Savage Mountain'.

K2 is also one of the hardest mountains in the world to climb. The first attempt to reach its summit was made in 1902 by the British climbers Aleister Crowley and Oscar Eckenstein, who reached 18,600 feet (5,670 metres). The summit was first reached on 31 July 1954 by the Italians Achille Compagnoni and Lino Lacedelli. The usual season for climbing is June, July or August, and for a long time K2 had never been climbed in winter; the first successful winter climb was completed on 26 February 2016 by Ali Sadpara of Pakistan, Alex Txikon and Simone Moro.

Pakistanis are justly proud of their own climbers on K2. Ashraf Aman became the first Pakistani to reach the summit on 9 August 1977, and on 26 July 2014 the first team of Pakistani climbers reached K2. The mountain is, however, extremely dangerous: till 2014, over 335 climbers had reached the summit while at least 82 people had died, giving a death rate of about 27 per cent. K2, therefore, is the pride of Pakistan - a beautiful but deadly mountain that has tested the courage of the world's best climbers for more than a century and has made the name of our country famous all over the world.
questions.explanation: This Study Skills exercise teaches the students to convert points into a connected essay. The model shows the paragraph plan, a general introduction about Pakistan that narrows down to K2, clear topic sentences, supporting details of three to five sentences in each paragraph, and a concluding paragraph that sums up the significance of the mountain.

questions.question: Exercise 2: Work individually and write an essay on Nanga Parbat, following the same steps as in Exercise 1. After you have completed, exchange your work with your partner, give each other feedback, revise your essay and write it in your notebook.
questions.answer:
Plan: The table information on Nanga Parbat divides into five paragraphs - (i) introduction on Pakistan and its northern mountains, (ii) location, height and range, (iii) the name and its meaning, (iv) climbing history and records, and (v) the danger and the conclusion.

Nanga Parbat: The Killer Mountain

Pakistan is a country of wonderful natural beauty, and its northern areas are famous all over the world for their lofty mountains, glaciers and green valleys. Among the giant peaks of the north, one of the most famous is Nanga Parbat, which stands like a white wall at the western end of the Himalayas. This essay presents the main facts about this great mountain.

Nanga Parbat is the ninth-highest mountain in the world and the second-highest mountain in Pakistan. It lies in the Northern Areas of Pakistan, between Chilas and Astore, in the district of Diamer, and it belongs to the Himalayan range. Its height is 8,126 metres, that is 26,660 feet, which makes it one of the highest mountains on the earth.

The mountain is known by several names. 'Nanga Parbat' literally means 'Naked Mountain', perhaps because its rocky summit is often swept bare of snow by fierce winds. Its local name is Diamer or Deo Mir, which means 'huge mountain'. These beautiful names hide, however, a very dangerous reality, for the mountain has earned a terrible nickname as well.

Nanga Parbat is called the 'Killer Mountain', and with good reason. The first attempt to climb it was made in 1895 by Albert F. Mummery and his team, who reached almost 6,100 metres (20,000 feet) but never returned. In all, 31 people died trying to climb the mountain before its first ascent. The summit was first reached on 3 July 1953 by the Austrian climber Hermann Buhl, in one of the greatest feats in the history of mountaineering. The mountain has since been climbed in both summer and winter; the first successful winter climb was made on 26 February 2016 by Ali Sadpara of Pakistan, Alex Txikon and Simone Moro. Even so, the mountain has taken a heavy toll: till 2012, at least 68 climbers had died on it, giving a death rate of 22.3 per cent.

Nanga Parbat, therefore, is both a wonder and a warning. It shows the immense beauty and the immense power of nature at the same time. The courage and sacrifice of the climbers who have attempted it, and especially of our own Pakistani mountaineers such as Ali Sadpara, have won honour for Pakistan and inspired thousands of young people to face difficulties with patience and daring.
questions.explanation: This exercise repeats the article-from-points skill of Exercise 1 with a new set of points about Nanga Parbat. The model again shows a paragraph plan, an introduction that moves from the general to the particular, topic sentences, supporting details and a conclusion.

questions.question: Doing Something Different: Think of one thing that you would like to do when you grow up; think of doing something different, something that people do not normally do. State what you will do, why you want to do it, and how you will do it. Then take a piece of paper and show what you will do, why you will do it and how, using writing, drawings or pictures and colours. Make your presentation bright and colourful. Afterwards, share your dream with the rest of the class by showing them your paper presentation.
questions.answer:
Model response (with a note of what to draw on the paper):

What I will do: When I grow up, I want to become a maker of musical instruments from waste materials - an 'eco-musician'. I would like to open a small workshop where broken buckets, old tins, bamboo, bottle tops and dry gourds are turned into drums, flutes, guitars and rattles for children.

Why I want to do it: I want to do this because it is something that people do not normally do. Most people throw away waste and buy new things, but I want to show that beautiful music can be created out of things that others call rubbish. In this way I can give poor children free musical instruments, keep our streets cleaner and reduce the harm that plastic waste does to our environment. Music also brings joy to people, and I want to spread that joy.

How I will do it: First, I will learn how musical instruments are made by watching video lessons and by requesting a local carpenter and a tabla maker to teach me in the holidays. Then I will collect waste material from shops and homes through a school campaign. In my workshop I will clean the material, cut and polish it safely, and fit strings, skins and pipes to make simple instruments. Finally, I will give these instruments to children and teach them in free weekly classes. In this way, waste will become music.

What to show on the paper: Divide the chart into three parts and label them 'WHAT', 'WHY' and 'HOW'.
- WHAT: draw a bright picture of my workshop with a guitar made from a tin, a drum from an old bucket and a flute from bamboo.
- WHY: write the three reasons - to make good use of waste, to reduce pollution and to bring free music to poor children.
- HOW: draw four small pictures showing the four steps - collecting waste, learning from elders, building the instruments and teaching the children. Use colour pencils and large clear headings so that the presentation looks bright and attractive.
questions.explanation: The Fun section is not formally assessed; its aim is to let the students enjoy the language while thinking out of the box. This model supplies the three required points (what, why, how) and also a concrete plan for the coloured paper presentation that the students must show to the class.

questions.question: Pre-reading: What is success?
questions.answer: Success means the achievement of a goal or the attainment of something we have worked hard for. For one person it may be passing an examination with good marks, for another it may be earning an honest living, helping others or becoming a good human being. In short, success is the happy result of honest effort, patience and determination, and it is measured not only by money or fame but also by the good we do for others.
questions.explanation: This pre-reading question asks students to share their own ideas about success before reading the story 'The Secret of Success'. There is no single correct answer; the aim is to activate prior knowledge.

questions.question: Exercise 1: The king asked the following people the three questions. Put them in the right order by writing the number in the blank space. (a. Common people, b. Ministers, c. Saint, d. Scholars and wise-man, e. King himself, f. Courtiers)
questions.answer:
Correct order (the order in which the king asked):
1. e. King himself (example - he first tried to answer the questions himself)
2. b. Ministers
3. f. Courtiers
4. d. Scholars and wise-man
5. a. Common people
6. c. Saint

So: a = 5, b = 2, c = 6, d = 4, e = 1, f = 3.
questions.explanation: In the story the king first thought about the questions himself, then called his ministers, next his courtiers, then the wise and learned men, then announced a reward so that common people could try, and finally visited the old saint.

questions.question: Exercise 2: Did the king find his answers?
questions.answer: Yes, the king did find his answers. Although the saint never replied to him in words, the events of the day and the saint's final explanation showed the king that his three questions had actually been answered.
questions.explanation: The saint answers the questions indirectly through the day's events and then explains them clearly after the bearded man leaves.

questions.question: Exercise 3: Read the text. Find the following words/phrases and underline them. (discover, evaded, disappointed, consult, pondered, destitute, frequently, determined, glanced, straight away, hospitality, break of day, bitter, grief, count on me, departed). Guess their meanings and check with the glossary.
questions.answer:
Meanings of the words/phrases: 
1. discover - to find out or come to know something for the first time. 
2. evaded - escaped or avoided (the answers evaded him = he could not find them). 
3. disappointed - sad because something was not as good as expected. 
4. consult - to ask someone for advice or information. 
5. pondered - thought about something carefully for a long time. 
6. destitute - extremely poor, having no money or possessions. 
7. frequently - often, many times. 
8. determined - having a strong wish to do something and not giving up. 
9. glanced - looked at something quickly. 
10. straight away - immediately, at once. 
11. hospitality - the friendly and generous treatment of guests. 
12. break of day - dawn, the time when daylight first appears. 
13. bitter - full of anger, hurt or hate (a bitter enemy). 
14. grief - deep sorrow, especially after someone's death. 
15. count on me - you can rely on me, trust me. 
16. departed - left, went away.
questions.explanation: These are the key vocabulary items from the story 'The Secret of Success'. Underlining them in the text and guessing the meanings from context is a vocabulary-building skill.

questions.question: Exercise 4: Work in pairs and see how many of the given words in Exercise 3 you can use in your own sentences.
questions.answer:
Model sentences: 
1. discover - Scientists hope to discover a cure for cancer one day. 
2. evaded - The thief evaded the police for many weeks. 
3. disappointed - I was disappointed when it rained on the day of the picnic. 
4. consult - You should consult a doctor before taking any medicine. 
5. pondered - She pondered over the difficult question for a long time. 
6. destitute - The flood left hundreds of families destitute. 
7. frequently - He frequently visits his grandmother on Sundays. 
8. determined - Sana was determined to win the race. 
9. glanced - The teacher glanced at her watch and hurried out. 
10. straight away - When I heard the news I went straight away to see my friend. 
11. hospitality - We thanked our hosts for their kind hospitality. 
12. break of day - The farmers set off for the fields at break of day. 
13. bitter - He became a bitter enemy of the man who cheated him. 
14. grief - The whole village was in grief after the accident. 
15. count on me - Do not worry about the money; you can always count on me. 
16. departed - The guests departed after dinner.
questions.explanation: The task encourages students to use the new words in their own sentences so that the vocabulary becomes active rather than passive.

questions.question: Exercise 5(a): The King wanted to find answers to 5 questions. Write T (true) or F (false).
questions.answer: False. The king wanted answers to three questions, not five: (1) the most important time to start something, (2) the most important work to do, and (3) the most important person.
questions.explanation: (a) is the worked example in the book and is marked F because the story mentions three questions.

questions.question: Exercise 6: Which one of the following statements best summarizes the story?
questions.answer: The best summary is (c) 'The present is the most important time.' The moral of the story is that the most important time for doing anything is the present, the most important work is what we are doing now, and the most important person is the one we are with.
questions.explanation: Option (c) matches the moral stated at the end of the story. The other options do not capture the full idea of the moral.

options.text: The present has all the answers.
The present is not what matters.
The present is the most important time.
The present gives you the most joy.

questions.optionsRaw: (a) The present has all the answers. (b) The present is not what matters. (c) The present is the most important time. (d) The present gives you the most joy.

questions.question: Exercise 7(a): The king wanted to find the answers to the three questions because ................
questions.answer: The king wanted to find the answers to the three questions because he thought that if he found out the answers, he would discover the secret of success and would never fail.
questions.explanation: The opening paragraph states the king's belief that the answers would reveal the secret of success.

questions.question: Exercise 8: Work in a group of 3-4 classmates and discuss whether the 'secret of success' is applicable to all people. Follow the steps: 1. Decide who will write the points. 2. Select the presenter. 3. Discuss if the 'secret of success' applies to all people or only to the king. 4. Give reasons for your point of view. 5. The writer writes down the reasons. 6. Select the points to be shared with the class.
questions.answer: Group discussion / model presentation. Steps carried out: (1) One member is chosen as the writer and (2) one as the presenter. (3) Conclusion of the group: the secret of success is applicable to ALL people. (4) Reasons: The three answers given by the saint are universal moral truths and not royal secrets. Firstly, the most important time is always the present - a farmer, a student, a doctor or a soldier all succeed only if they act honestly in the present moment instead of waiting for tomorrow. Secondly, the most important work is always the duty in hand - studying for a student, treating a patient for a doctor, or helping a neighbour for anyone. Thirdly, the most important person is the one we are with at that moment, because kindness to those around us builds trust and wins friends. (5) The writer notes down these reasons, and (6) the presenter shares these points, concluding that success comes from doing our present duty with sincerity towards the person in front of us, whatever our age or occupation.
questions.explanation: This is a group-speaking task; the model answer shows the required steps and a reasoned point of view. Students may support the opposite view (that it applied only to the king) but must give reasons.

questions.question: Pre-reading: What are the qualities of a successful person?
questions.answer: A successful person usually has the following qualities: hard work, honesty, patience, determination, self-confidence, punctuality and discipline. Such a person sets clear goals, plans carefully, learns from failures and never loses hope. He is kind and helpful to others, respects people, keeps his word, manages his time well and keeps trying until the task is complete.
questions.explanation: Students are expected to list the personal qualities they associate with success. Answers will vary but should show understanding of good character and effort.

questions.question: Exercise 2: Who gave him the answers?
questions.answer: The old saint (the wise man who lived alone in the jungle) gave him the answers. He explained that the most important time was when the king helped him, the most important work was digging the ground and then dressing the wounded man's wound, and the most important person was the one he was with at that moment.
questions.explanation: The saint's reply at the end of the story provides the answers to all three of the king's questions.

questions.question: Exercise 5(b): The answers were important for him to be able to control his army.
questions.answer: False. The king wanted the answers because he believed they would reveal the secret of success and help him never fail in life; there is no mention of controlling his army.
questions.explanation: The text says the king 'was in search of the secret of success' and 'would discover the secret and never fail'.

questions.question: Exercise 6: The saint who lived in the jungle was a very:
questions.answer: The correct answer is (d) wise man. The text calls him 'an old wise man who was considered a saint'.
questions.explanation: The story repeatedly describes the saint as wise and learned, famous for solving everyone's problems.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) rich man (b) poor man (c) severe man (d) wise man

questions.question: Exercise 7(b): The wise and learned men were unable to give the answers because ................
questions.answer: The wise and learned men were unable to give the answers because they could not see eye to eye with each other and ended up arguing among themselves; none of their many answers provided any meaningful solution.
questions.explanation: The text explains that the learned men disagreed and quarrelled instead of agreeing on an answer.

questions.question: Pre-reading: How do you think you could become successful?
questions.answer: I could become successful by setting clear and realistic goals, working hard and never giving up, managing my time well and studying regularly. I would stay honest, help others whenever I can, listen to the advice of my elders and teachers, and learn from my mistakes. Most importantly, I would focus on the present moment and do my best work with the people who are with me now.
questions.explanation: The question invites personal reflection. The final point links nicely with the moral of the story, which is that the most important time is now and the most important person is the one we are with.

questions.question: Exercise 5(c): The king was looking for the answers in order to succeed in life.
questions.answer: True. The king was searching for the secret of success so that he would never fail, that is, so that he could succeed in life.
questions.explanation: The opening lines state that the king 'was in search of the secret of success' and thought the three answers would make him 'never fail'.

questions.question: Exercise 6: The king went to see the saint:
questions.answer: The correct answer is (a) all alone. The king dressed himself in rags and asked his servants to remain behind, so he went alone.
questions.explanation: The text says: 'he asked his servants to remain behind. Alone, he headed straight for the saint's hut.'
questions.optionsRaw: (a) all alone (b) with all his soldiers (c) along with his family (d) with all his courtiers

questions.question: Exercise 7(c): The king dressed himself in rags to meet the saint because ................
questions.answer: The king dressed himself in rags to meet the saint because the saint did not like meeting wealthy people and only mixed with the poor and needy, so the king wanted to appear poor and destitute.
questions.explanation: The story tells us the saint avoided the rich and helped the poor, which is why the king changed his appearance.

questions.question: Exercise 5(d): The king was happy with the answers that the group of learned men found.
questions.answer: False. The wise and learned men could not satisfy the king; they could not see eye to eye with each other, argued among themselves and provided no meaningful solution.
questions.explanation: The text clearly states that the learned men 'were unable to satisfy the king'.

questions.question: Exercise 6: Who warned the king that the bearded man was coming?
questions.answer: The correct answer is (b) the saint. The saint remained silent and pointed to one side, showing the king that the bearded man was running towards them.
questions.explanation: The saint 'remained silent and pointed to one side', drawing the king's attention to the running man.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) his soldiers (b) the saint (c) his servants (d) his minister

questions.question: Exercise 7(d): The king told his servants not to go with him because ................
questions.answer: The king told his servants not to go with him because he wanted to appear poor and destitute before the saint; if servants had accompanied him, he would not have looked like a poor man.
questions.explanation: The king planned to disguise himself as a poor man, so he left his servants behind.

questions.question: Exercise 5(e): The saint was living in the jungle with his family.
questions.answer: False. The saint lived in the jungle all alone; the text says 'He lived all alone'.
questions.explanation: The story describes the saint as an old wise man who lived by himself in the jungle.

questions.question: Exercise 6: After the bearded man left the saint told the king that:
questions.answer: The correct answer is (d) all his questions had been answered. The saint explained that the day's events had already answered the king's three questions.
questions.explanation: The saint says: 'Your questions have already been answered.'

options.text: he would not answer his questions
the bearded man had answered his questions
all his questions had been answered

questions.optionsRaw: (a) he would not answer his questions (b) his questions were too difficult (c) the bearded man had answered his questions (d) all his questions had been answered

questions.question: Exercise 7(e): The king realized the saint tired easily because ................
questions.answer: The king realized the saint tired easily because the saint was old and weak; as he dug the ground he was breathing hard, and he stopped frequently to rest.
questions.explanation: The text describes the saint as old and weak and frequently stopping to rest while digging.

questions.question: Exercise 5(f): The king accepted the saint's invitation to visit him in the jungle.
questions.answer: False. It was the king who decided on his own to consult the saint; the saint had not invited him. (The saint did later invite the king to stay the night in his hut, but he never invited him to the jungle.)
questions.explanation: The king 'decided to consult the wise old saint' and dressed in rags to approach him; no invitation from the saint is mentioned.

questions.question: Exercise 7(f): Although the saint did not answer his questions the king waited because ................
questions.answer: Although the saint did not answer his questions the king waited because he hoped that he would find the answers to his questions; this hope kept him motivated and determined.
questions.explanation: The text says 'The hope that he would find the answers to his questions, kept him motivated and determined.'

questions.question: Exercise 5(g): The bearded man wanted to kill the king.
questions.answer: True. The bearded man confessed that he had come to kill the king because he believed the king had had his brother killed.
questions.explanation: The bearded man says: 'Forgive me, I came to kill you because you had had my brother killed.'

questions.question: Exercise 7(g): The bearded man was running towards the king because ................
questions.answer: The bearded man was running towards the king because he wanted to kill him, as he believed the king had had his brother killed and he had become the king's bitter enemy out of grief.
questions.explanation: The bearded man later confesses his intention to take revenge for his brother's death.

questions.question: Exercise 5(h): The bearded man had been injured by the king's servants.
questions.answer: True. The bearded man explains that when he came out of his hiding place the king's servants recognised him and wounded him seriously.
questions.explanation: He says: 'They wounded me seriously but I escaped.'

questions.question: Exercise 7(h): The bearded man fainted when he reached the king because ................
questions.answer: The bearded man fainted when he reached the king because he had been wounded seriously by the king's servants and had lost a great deal of blood.
questions.explanation: The man was badly injured after being recognised and wounded by the king's servants.

questions.question: Exercise 5(i): The saint asked the king to look after the bearded man.
questions.answer: False. The saint did not ask the king to look after the bearded man. He only remained silent and pointed to one side; the king himself saw the wounded man and looked after him on his own.
questions.explanation: The saint 'remained silent and pointed to one side', after which the king acted of his own accord.

questions.question: Exercise 7(i): The king agreed to stay the night in the saint's hut because ................
questions.answer: The king agreed to stay the night in the saint's hut because night had fallen and it was very dark, and he was too tired to return home; the saint had kindly offered him hospitality.
questions.explanation: The text explains that by now night had fallen and the king was too tired to return home.

questions.question: Exercise 5(j): The bearded man became the king's loyal citizen.
questions.answer: True. After the king saved his life the bearded man saluted him and said, 'Now, count on me as one of your most faithful servants.' In this way he became loyal to the king.
questions.explanation: The book uses the word 'citizen' while the text says 'faithful servant'; either way the man pledged his loyalty to the king, so the statement is true.

questions.question: Exercise 7(j): The bearded man became the king's loyal servant because ................
questions.answer: The bearded man became the king's loyal servant because the king had saved his life: he had picked him up, carried him into the hut, stopped the bleeding and bandaged his wounds. Grateful for this kindness, he gave up his enmity and promised to serve the king faithfully.
questions.explanation: The king's merciful treatment of his enemy won the man's loyalty, which is also part of the story's message.

questions.question: Exercise 1 (Topic 1): Prepare a two-minute speech on 'Water problem' following the steps given.
questions.answer:
Model two-minute speech - Water Problem: 
Introduction: Good morning, respected teacher and dear friends. Today I want to speak about one of the biggest problems of our city - the water problem. 
Point 1: Shortage of clean water - Our taps run dry for most of the day, and the little water we get is often dirty and unfit for drinking. 
Point 2: Causes - Old and leaking pipelines, careless use of water, and the fast-growing population are the main reasons for this shortage. 
Point 3: Effects and solutions - Dirty water causes diseases like cholera and typhoid, and women and children have to walk long distances to fetch water. We should repair leaking pipes, use water carefully, harvest rainwater and stop wasting this precious gift of nature. 
Conclusion: Every drop of water is precious. If we all act responsibly today, we can save clean water for tomorrow. Thank you.
questions.explanation: This follows the book's step-by-step speech plan: introduce yourself, introduce the topic, state and explain three points with reasons, and conclude by restating the main points.

questions.question: Exercise 2 (Topic 1): Prepare a two-minute assembly speech on 'Cheating' following all the steps and directions given in Exercise 1.
questions.answer:
Model two-minute assembly speech - Cheating: 
Introduction: Respectable teachers and dear students, good morning. Today I am going to speak to you about a habit that harms us more than it helps us - cheating. 
Point 1: What cheating is - Cheating means being dishonest to gain unfair advantage - in examinations, games, or in money matters. 
Point 2: Why it is harmful - A student who cheats may pass an exam, but he never learns anything and loses the trust of everyone. Cheating weakens character and destroys self-confidence. 
Point 3: How to avoid it - We should prepare honestly for our tests, seek help from teachers when we do not understand something, and remember that true success comes only from hard work and honesty. 
Conclusion: Honesty is the best policy. Let us all promise to earn our success the honest way. Thank you.
questions.explanation: An assembly talk following the same public-speaking conventions: greeting, topic introduction, three developed points, and a concluding reminder.

questions.question: Exercise 1 (Topic 2): Prepare a two-minute speech on 'Electricity shortage' following the steps given.
questions.answer:
Model two-minute speech - Electricity Shortage: 
Introduction: Good morning, respected teacher and dear friends. My topic today is the shortage of electricity in our country. 
Point 1: The problem - Long, unannounced power cuts are a part of our daily life. In summer we suffer for many hours without fans or lights. 
Point 2: Causes - Our demand for electricity is far greater than the supply, and much of our old equipment and transmission system wastes energy. Too few power stations and heavy line losses add to the problem. 
Point 3: Effects and solutions - The shortage closes factories, spoils food in refrigerators, disturbs studies and creates great hardship for the sick and the elderly. We must generate more electricity from water, coal and solar energy, stop electricity theft, and use energy wisely by switching off unnecessary lights and appliances. 
Conclusion: Electricity is the backbone of modern life. Saving it and producing it wisely is our national duty. Thank you.
questions.explanation: A complete two-minute speech outline following the conventions of public speaking taught in this unit.

questions.question: Exercise 2 (Topic 2): Prepare a two-minute assembly speech on 'Regularity and punctuality' following all the steps and directions given in Exercise 1.
questions.answer:
Model two-minute assembly speech - Regularity and Punctuality: 
Introduction: Respected teachers and dear fellow students, good morning. My topic today is regularity and punctuality. 
Point 1: Meaning - Regularity means doing things at the right times every day without missing them, and punctuality means being on time. 
Point 2: Why it matters - A student who comes regularly and on time keeps pace with his lessons, and a punctual person is trusted everywhere in life. 
Point 3: How to practise it - We should make a timetable, sleep and wake up on time, finish homework daily, and reach school and every appointment a little before time. 
Conclusion: Time once lost never comes back; regularity and punctuality build success, discipline and a good reputation. Thank you.
questions.explanation: Model assembly speech following the steps of Exercise 1.

questions.question: Exercise 1 (Topic 3): Prepare a two-minute speech on 'Sewerage system' following the steps given.
questions.answer:
Model two-minute speech - Sewerage System: 
Introduction: Good morning, respected teacher and dear friends. Today I shall speak about the poor sewerage system in our towns. 
Point 1: The problem - Drains in many of our streets overflow, and dirty water stands in the open, spreading a bad smell all around. 
Point 2: Causes - Broken and blocked drains, careless dumping of rubbish into them, and poor maintenance by the authorities are the main causes. 
Point 3: Effects and solutions - Standing sewerage water breeds mosquitoes and spreads diseases like malaria, typhoid and diarrhoea, especially among children. The authorities must clean and repair the drains regularly, and we citizens must not throw plastic bags and rubbish into them. 
Conclusion: A clean sewerage system means a healthy city. Clean surroundings begin with our own responsible habits. Thank you.
questions.explanation: Follows the required speech structure and gives supporting details for each point.

questions.question: Exercise 2 (Topic 3): Prepare a two-minute assembly speech on 'Discipline' following all the steps and directions given in Exercise 1.
questions.answer:
Model two-minute assembly speech - Discipline: 
Introduction: Respected teachers and dear friends, good morning. Today I want to talk to you about discipline. 
Point 1: Meaning - Discipline means obeying the right rules, following good order and controlling oneself. 
Point 2: Why it matters - There is discipline in nature - the sun rises on time and the seasons change on time. A school, a team, an army or a nation succeeds only because of discipline. 
Point 3: Our duty - We must respect our teachers and elders, obey the rules of the school, keep our class clean, wait for our turn, and control our anger and laziness. 
Conclusion: Discipline is the bridge between goals and success. A disciplined student today becomes a disciplined and successful citizen tomorrow. Thank you.
questions.explanation: A structured assembly speech with introduction, three supported points and conclusion.

questions.question: Exercise 1 (Topic 4): Prepare a two-minute speech on 'Waste disposal' following the steps given.
questions.answer:
Model two-minute speech - Waste Disposal: 
Introduction: Good morning, respected teacher and dear friends. I shall speak today about the improper disposal of waste. 
Point 1: The problem - Garbage heaps can be seen at street corners, and people often burn or throw waste in open places. 
Point 2: Causes - The growing quantity of household and factory waste, careless habits, and a lack of proper dustbins and collection services cause this problem. 
Point 3: Effects and solutions - Rotting waste produces a foul smell, breeds flies and mosquitoes, and pollutes the air, soil and water. We should separate our waste, use dustbins, recycle paper, plastic and metal, and encourage our neighbours to keep the streets clean. 
Conclusion: The cleanliness of our city depends upon how we throw our waste. Let us make 'No to littering' our habit. Thank you.
questions.explanation: Model speech showing the introduction, three developed points with examples and a concluding statement.

questions.question: Exercise 2 (Topic 4): Prepare a two-minute assembly speech on 'Cleanliness' following all the steps and directions given in Exercise 1.
questions.answer:
Model two-minute assembly speech - Cleanliness: 
Introduction: Respected teachers and dear students, good morning. My topic for today is cleanliness. 
Point 1: Why it matters - Cleanliness is not only a good habit, it also protects us from many diseases. 
Point 2: The problem - Dirty classrooms, littered playgrounds, and unclean streets and hands are common sights, and they cause illness. 
Point 3: Our duty - We should wash our hands before eating, keep our classroom and school clean, throw rubbish into dustbins, and remember that 'cleanliness is half of faith'. 
Conclusion: If each one of us keeps his own corner clean, the whole school and the whole country will shine. Let us take up cleanliness as a habit, not a one-day task. Thank you.
questions.explanation: Model assembly speech showing the three-point structure and a concluding appeal.

questions.question: Exercise 1 (Topic 5): Prepare a two-minute speech on 'Education system' following the steps given.
questions.answer:
Model two-minute speech - Education System: 
Introduction: Good morning, respected teacher and dear friends. Today I would like to speak about our education system. 
Point 1: The problem - Many children in our country are still out of school, and those who study often learn by rote instead of understanding. 
Point 2: Causes - Poverty, shortage of trained teachers, overcrowded classrooms, old teaching methods and a lack of proper facilities are the main reasons. 
Point 3: Effects and solutions - A weak education system produces an unskilled nation that cannot compete in the modern world. We need well-trained teachers, modern and practical teaching methods, better school facilities and free education for every child. 
Conclusion: Education is the strongest weapon with which we can change our future. Improving it must be our first priority. Thank you.
questions.explanation: Model speech with a clear introduction, three supported points and a memorable conclusion.

questions.question: Exercise 2 (Topic 5): Prepare a two-minute assembly speech on 'Games and sports' following all the steps and directions given in Exercise 1.
questions.answer:
Model two-minute assembly speech - Games and Sports: 
Introduction: Respected teachers and dear friends, good morning. Today I shall speak about the value of games and sports. 
Point 1: Why we need them - Games and sports keep our body healthy, our mind fresh and our energy well used. 
Point 2: Benefits - They teach us teamwork, discipline, patience and the spirit to accept defeat. A healthy body also helps a healthy mind to study better. 
Point 3: Our role - Every student should take part in at least one game or sport, whether cricket, football, badminton or athletics. We should play on the playground rather than waste time on mobile phones. 
Conclusion: 'A sound mind in a sound body.' Let us all play games and grow up healthy and strong. Thank you.
questions.explanation: Model assembly talk following the required public-speaking structure.

questions.question: Exercise 1 (Topic 6): Prepare a two-minute speech on 'Health Facilities' following the steps given.
questions.answer:
Model two-minute speech - Health Facilities: 
Introduction: Good morning, respected teacher and dear friends. My topic today is the health facilities in our country. 
Point 1: The problem - In many villages and even in some city areas there is no proper hospital, no qualified doctor and no life-saving medicines for the poor. 
Point 2: Causes - Limited health budget, shortage of doctors and nurses in rural areas, and the high cost of private treatment keep basic health care out of reach for ordinary people. 
Point 3: Effects and solutions - Because of poor facilities, many patients die of diseases that could easily be cured. The government must build more hospitals and basic health units, post trained doctors in villages, supply free medicines and hold public awareness and vaccination campaigns. 
Conclusion: A healthy nation is a strong nation. Good health facilities are the right of every citizen. Thank you.
questions.explanation: Follows the public-speaking convention of stating and then supporting each point with reasons and examples.

questions.question: Exercise 2 (Topic 6): Prepare a two-minute assembly speech on 'Team work' following all the steps and directions given in Exercise 1.
questions.answer:
Model two-minute assembly speech - Team Work: 
Introduction: Respected teachers and dear students, good morning. My topic today is team work. 
Point 1: Meaning - Team work means working together, sharing duties and helping one another to reach a common goal. 
Point 2: Why it matters - Many hands make light work. A cricket team wins because every player supports the others, and a class succeeds because all the students co-operate. 
Point 3: Our duty - We should share our work fairly, listen to others, value every member's contribution, and not try to shine alone at the cost of the group. 
Conclusion: Where there is unity, there is strength. If we work as a team, no task is too difficult for us. Thank you.
questions.explanation: Model assembly speech with introduction, three developed points and a suitable conclusion.

questions.question: Exercise 1 (Topic 7): Prepare a two-minute speech on '14th August' following the steps given.
questions.answer:
Model two-minute speech - 14th August: 
Introduction: Good morning, respected teacher and dear friends. Today I shall speak about the importance of the 14th of August, our Independence Day. 
Point 1: What it means - On this day in 1947, after great sacrifices, our forefathers won for us a free homeland, Pakistan. 
Point 2: The price of freedom - Over a million people laid down their lives, and millions had to leave their homes so that Muslims could live freely according to their faith. 
Point 3: Our duty today - The 14th of August reminds us to be thankful and to renew our promise to work honestly for the progress of our country. We should hoist the flag, sing the national anthem and remember the heroes of the freedom movement. 
Conclusion: Freedom is a great blessing earned through sacrifice; we must protect and value it by being good, hardworking citizens. Thank you.
questions.explanation: A model patriotic speech following the required speech structure.

questions.question: Exercise 1 (Topic 8): Prepare a two-minute speech on 'Literacy day' following the steps given.
questions.answer:
Model two-minute speech - International Literacy Day: 
Introduction: Good morning, respected teacher and dear friends. Today I want to speak about International Literacy Day, which is observed every year on the 8th of September. 
Point 1: What it is - It is a day on which the whole world reminds itself of the value of reading and writing. 
Point 2: Why it matters - Millions of people in our country still cannot read or write, and an uneducated person cannot understand his rights, take care of his health or earn a good living. 
Point 3: Our role - On this day we should take part in literacy drives, teach at least one illiterate person around us, and encourage parents to send their children, especially their daughters, to school. 
Conclusion: Literacy is the first step towards progress. Let every one of us promise to spread the light of education. Thank you.
questions.explanation: Model speech that introduces the topic, gives three developed points and concludes with a suggestion, as required.

questions.question: Exercise 1 (Topic 9): Prepare a two-minute speech on 'Plantation' following the steps given.
questions.answer:
Model two-minute speech - Plantation: 
Introduction: Good morning, respected teacher and dear friends. I shall speak today about the importance of planting trees. 
Point 1: Why trees matter - Trees give us oxygen, cool the air, prevent soil erosion and provide shade, fruit and timber. 
Point 2: The problem - Our country has very little forest cover, and thousands of trees are cut down every day for wood and building materials. 
Point 3: Effects and solutions - Deforestation causes floods, heat and drought, and it harms our climate and health. We should take part in tree-planting campaigns, discourage unnecessary cutting of trees and look after the saplings we plant. 
Conclusion: 'If you cut a tree, plant two.' Let us all plant at least one tree each and make our land green again. Thank you.
questions.explanation: Complete model speech with introduction, three supported points and a concluding appeal.

questions.question: Exercise 1 (Topic 10): Prepare a two-minute speech on 'Wild Life Protection' following the steps given.
questions.answer:
Model two-minute speech - Wild Life Protection: 
Introduction: Good morning, respected teacher and dear friends. Today my topic is the protection of wild life. 
Point 1: What wild life is - Wild animals and birds are an important part of nature and keep our environment in balance. 
Point 2: The danger - Because of hunting, cutting of forests and pollution, many species of animals and birds are disappearing, and some are already extinct. 
Point 3: Effects and solutions - When one species is lost, the whole natural balance is disturbed. The government must enforce strict laws against hunting, create national parks and reserves, and we must say no to animal products and cruelty to animals. 
Conclusion: Animals and birds are our fellow creatures; protecting them means protecting our own future. Thank you.
questions.explanation: Model speech that follows the required plan of introducing, explaining and concluding the topic.

questions.question: Translation introduction: Translate the following sentences into Urdu/Sindhi, noticing how the word 'spring' has a different meaning in each. (a) I will go to Murree in spring. (b) There is a spring of hot water at Manghopir, in Karachi. (c) Since a spring is broken, this clock is not working. (d) With a spring, the runner crossed the winning line.)
questions.answer: These examples show that the same English word can have different meanings in different contexts, so it cannot be translated word for word. Meanings of 'spring': (a) the season of spring; (b) a natural fountain or source of water; (c) a coiled metal part of a machine; (d) a jump or leap. Urdu translations: (a) میں بہار کے موسم میں مری جاؤں گا۔ (b) کراچی کے منگھوپیر میں گرم پانی کا چشمہ ہے۔ (c) چونکہ اس گھڑی کی کمانی ٹوٹی ہوئی ہے، اس لیے یہ چل نہیں رہی۔ (d) دوڑنے والا ایک جست لگا کر جیت کی لکیر عبور کر گیا۔
questions.explanation: The introductory examples prepare students for the fact that translation depends on meaning and context, not merely on words.

questions.question: Exercise 1: Translate into Urdu/Sindhi: 'The train left the station at 7 o'clock.'
questions.answer: ٹرین سات بجے اسٹیشن سے روانہ ہوئی۔ (Here 'train' is a noun meaning a railway train = ٹرین۔) Sindhi: ريل گاڏي ستين وڳي اسٽيشن تان رواني ٿي.
questions.explanation: In this sentence 'train' is used as a noun. Compare it with sentence 2 where 'train' is a verb.

questions.question: Exercise 2: Translate into Urdu/Sindhi bringing out the real meaning: 'The sun peaked happily from behind the clouds.'
questions.answer: Real meaning: The sun came out from behind the clouds and shone brightly. Urdu: سورج بادلوں کے پیچھے سے خوشی سے جھانکا / چمکا۔ Sindhi: سجڪڙي ڪڪرن جي پويان کان خوشيءَ سان چهنب ڪڍي.
questions.explanation: The sun is personified as a happy person peeping out; the figurative 'happily' simply suggests bright, cheerful sunshine.

questions.question: Exercise 3: Translation competition between groups. Each group selects 10 sentences from the story 'The Secret of Success', writes them on paper, and the groups exchange papers and translate the sentences into Urdu/Sindhi. A point is given for each correct translation.
questions.answer: Model answer showing how the competition is carried out: (1) The teacher divides the class into groups of four and writes each group's name on the board. (2) Each group chooses 10 sentences from 'The Secret of Success', for example: 'A long time ago there lived a king who was in search of the secret of success.'; 'He called all his ministers.'; 'The saint was digging the ground in front of his hut.'; 'The king started digging.'; 'The king noticed that the man was injured.'; 'The king immediately took steps to stop the bleeding.'; 'The bearded man fell into a deep restful sleep.'; 'The saint prepared some simple food.'; 'The most important time is the present.'; 'The most important person is the one whom we are with at the moment.' (3) The papers are collected and redistributed. (4) Each group translates the sentences it receives into Urdu or Sindhi, for example: 'بہت عرصہ پہلے ایک بادشاہ رہتا تھا جو کامیابی کا راز تلاش کر رہا تھا۔'; 'سب سے اہم وقت موجودہ وقت ہے۔' (5) One member of each group reads out the sentence and its translation, and (6) a point is awarded for every correct translation. The group with the most points wins.
questions.explanation: This is a group translation game. The model answer lists the steps and gives sample sentences and their translations so that students can play the game.

questions.question: Exercise 4(A): Fill in the blank using the prefix 'un' with the appropriate word (happy, friendly, wise, healthy, grateful): 'An ______ person often falls sick.'
questions.answer: An unhealthy person often falls sick.
questions.explanation: The prefix 'un-' means 'not'; 'unhealthy' fits because such a person falls sick often.

questions.question: Translation introduction: Translate literally, then give the real meaning and translate: 'She has a sweet tooth.'
questions.answer: Literal translation (word for word): اس کے ایک میٹھا دانت ہے۔ Real meaning: She loves sweet things / she is very fond of sweets. Meaningful Urdu translation: اسے میٹھی چیزوں سے بہت شوق ہے۔
questions.explanation: The idiom 'a sweet tooth' cannot be translated literally; it means a great liking for sweet food. Students must bring out the real meaning in the translation.

questions.question: Exercise 1: Translate into Urdu/Sindhi: 'I can train you to become a good cricketer.'
questions.answer: میں تمہیں ایک اچھا کرکٹر بننے کی تربیت دے سکتا ہوں۔ (Here 'train' is a verb meaning to teach or coach = تربیت دینا۔) Sindhi: مان توھان کي سٺو ڪرڪيٽر بنجڻ جي تربيت ڏئي سگهان ٿو.
questions.explanation: 'Train' here is a verb, showing that the same word can function as different parts of speech and must be translated by meaning.

questions.question: Exercise 2: Translate into Urdu/Sindhi bringing out the real meaning: 'The trees danced back and forth in the wind.'
questions.answer: Real meaning: The trees swayed to and fro in the wind. Urdu: درخت ہوا میں آگے پیچھے ناچتے / جھومتے رہے۔ Sindhi: وڻ هوا ۾ اڳتي پوئتي نچندا رهيا.
questions.explanation: The trees do not really dance; the word describes their swinging movement in the wind (personification).

questions.question: Exercise 4(A): 'Saba is very ______ and does not like meeting people.' (happy, friendly, wise, healthy, grateful)
questions.answer: Saba is very unfriendly and does not like meeting people.
questions.explanation: 'Unfriendly' means not friendly, which matches her dislike of meeting people.
