questions.question: Exercise 3: Read the poem 'The Miller of the Dee' by Charles Mackay silently, then discuss the story with your partner. (What is the poem about? Who are the characters? What happens between them?)
questions.answer: Model discussion of the story: The poem tells the story of two characters - a poor but cheerful miller who lives and works beside the river Dee, and King Hal, a rich and powerful ruler who is unhappy. The miller works and sings happily from morning till night and boasts that he envies nobody and nobody envies him. King Hal hears him and says, 'Thou'rt wrong, my friend!' telling him that if his own heart were as light as the miller's he would gladly change places with him, and he asks what makes the miller sing so freely while the king himself is sad. The miller answers, smiling and doffing his cap, that he earns his bread honestly, loves his wife, his friend and his three children, owes no penny he cannot pay, and thanks the river Dee which turns his mill and grinds the corn that feeds his family. The king sighs and admits that no one envies the miller, that the miller's simple cap is worth his crown and his mill worth his kingdom, for such contented and honest men are the pride of England. So the poem shows that true happiness lies in honest labour and contentment, not in wealth or power.
questions.explanation: This is a pre-writing discussion task. The model outlines the poem's story - the happy miller, the envious king, their conversation and the king's final admission - which the students will later turn into a full summary in Exercise 4.

questions.question: Exercise 4: After discussing the story orally in pairs, write the story of the poem 'The Miller of the Dee' in your own words as a summary. Follow the given steps: give the title of the poem and the name of the poet, write the key message, and then write the story in your own words (you may use dialogues in direct speech).
questions.answer:
Summary of 'The Miller of the Dee' by Charles Mackay

The poem 'The Miller of the Dee' is written by Charles Mackay. It tells the story of a poor but cheerful miller who lives beside the river Dee and of the rich and powerful King Hal who is unhappy despite his wealth.

There lived a miller, healthy and bold, beside the river Dee. He worked and sang happily from morning till night, and no bird was more cheerful than he. The burden of his song, which he sang again and again, was: "I envy nobody, no, not I, and nobody envies me!"

Hearing him, King Hal said, "Thou'rt wrong, my friend! Thou'rt wrong as wrong can be. For, could my heart be light as thine, I'd gladly change with thee." The king then asked him what made him sing so loudly and freely, while he himself was sad even though he was a king, beside the river Dee.

The miller smiled, doffed his cap and replied: "I earn my bread, I love my wife, I love my friend, I love my children three. I owe no penny I cannot pay; I thank the river Dee that turns the mill that grinds the corn to feed my babes and me."

King Hal then sighed awhile and said: "Good friend! Farewell, and happy be; but say no more, if thou'dst say true, that no man envies thee. Thy mealy cap is worth my crown, thy mill my kingdom's fee; such men as thou are England's boast, O miller of the Dee!"

Key message: The poem teaches us that true happiness does not depend on wealth, power or high position but on honest labour, contentment, love of family and freedom from debt. The poor miller is happier than the king because he is satisfied with what he has, and such simple, honest and contented people are the real pride of their country.
questions.explanation: The summary begins with the title and the poet's name, states the key message, and then retells the whole story stanza by stanza in the student's own words using direct speech for the dialogues.

questions.question: Exercise (a): Work in groups of three and prepare a presentation on the topic assigned to you by the teacher, deciding who will deliver which part. Practise giving the presentation as a group before presenting it in front of the class. Topics: 1. The importance of female education 2. Drive Safety 3. Punctuality in work and studies 4. Cleanliness: self and surroundings 5. The role that citizens can play in building a good society.
questions.answer:
Model presentation outline for Topic 1, 'The importance of female education' (a group of three divides the presentation into three parts):

Part 1 (Introduction - by student A): Greeting and topic statement. 'Educating a girl educates a family, a community and a nation.' An educated woman can read and write, take care of her health, guide her children and earn a living. In Pakistan, female literacy is still low, so this is an urgent issue.

Part 2 (Main points - by student B): (i) Educated mothers raise healthier and better-educated children. (ii) Educated women can get jobs and support their families, which reduces poverty. (iii) Education gives women confidence, awareness of their rights and protection from exploitation. (iv) Countries that educate their women develop faster.

Part 3 (Conclusion and call to action - by student C): Educating girls is not a favour to women but a necessity for the whole nation. Schools should be made safe and accessible for girls, and families and parents should be encouraged to send their daughters to school. Concluding line: 'If you educate a man you educate an individual, but if you educate a woman you educate a whole generation.'

Steps followed (from the text): brainstorm the topic, identify the theme and focus, structure the ideas logically, support the subject with facts, prepare cue cards, and finally deliver the presentation with good body language and eye contact.

Model cue card: Topic - Importance of female education; Part 1 - greet, define topic, one fact (low female literacy in Pakistan); Part 2 - four benefits (health, income, awareness, national growth); Part 3 - conclusion and call to action.
questions.explanation: This study-skills task builds the steps of preparing and giving a group presentation: brainstorming, choosing a focus, organising points logically, supporting them with facts and cue cards, and delivering them as a team.

questions.question: Exercise (b): While each group gives its presentation, the rest of the class should evaluate it on the given criteria - Topic and points clearly stated; Organization of ideas; Supporting details; Body language (use of facial expressions, gestures); Eye contact - rating each item as Exceptional, Admirable, Acceptable or Attempted.
questions.answer:
Model peer evaluation of a presentation, using the four-point scale (Exceptional = very good, Admirable = good, Acceptable = average, Attempted = needed improvement):

1. Topic and points clearly stated - Admirable: the speakers introduced the topic well and the main points were easy to follow.
2. Organization of ideas - Exceptional: there was a clear beginning, middle and end, and each member spoke in turn without confusion.
3. Supporting details - Acceptable: some facts were given, but more examples and figures would have made the arguments stronger.
4. Body language (facial expressions, gestures) - Admirable: the speakers used appropriate gestures and looked natural and confident.
5. Eye contact - Attempted: one speaker read continuously from the notes and rarely looked at the audience; therefore improvement is needed here.

Overall comment: The group's presentation was good and well organised, but they should add more supporting facts and improve their eye contact by using cue cards instead of full scripts.
questions.explanation: The evaluation table on page 200 asks listeners to judge each presentation against five criteria on a four-point scale. The model shows how to give a fair, specific and constructive comment for each criterion.

questions.question: Acting out a poem: Work in groups of five and act out the stanza of the poem 'The Daffodils' by William Wordsworth allotted to your group, in the form of a tableau. One student reads out the stanza while the other four act it out. Prepare in ten minutes, then perform, following the steps given (read the poem, choose a reciter, decide who will do what and rehearse).
questions.answer:
Model tableau plan for Stanza 1 of 'The Daffodils' (the group has five students - one reciter and four actors):

Reciter (Student 1) reads aloud: 'I wandered lonely as a cloud / That floats on high o'er vales and hills, / When all at once I saw a crowd, / A host of golden daffodils; / Beside the lake, beneath the trees, / Fluttering and dancing in the breeze.'

Actor 2 (the wanderer): walks slowly and sadly across the 'stage' with head bent, like a lonely cloud, then suddenly stops and looks up in surprise.

Actor 3 (the lake): stands still with arms curved and gently moving to suggest the calm water.

Actor 4 (a tree): stands with arms raised and swaying to show the branches beneath which the daffodils grow.

Actor 5 (the daffodils): stands among the others with both hands held up and swaying side to side, 'fluttering and dancing in the breeze'.

Tableau (freeze): at the end of the stanza all four actors freeze in place - the wanderer gazing in wonder at the swaying daffodils beside the still lake under the tree - holding the picture for a few seconds. No words are used by the actors, because a tableau is a scene acted out without speech; only the reciter speaks.

Steps followed: (1) read the whole poem and discussed how best to act out the stanza; (2) selected one person to recite the stanza while the other four act it out; (3) decided who would do what and rehearsed quickly.
questions.explanation: A tableau is a silent 'living picture' in which actors use only posture and movement while a single student recites the stanza. The plan assigns a clear role to each of the five group members and ends in a frozen picture.

questions.question: Task 1: Identify 7-10 adjectives and adverbs used in the text 'The Healthy Living'. Use them in your own sentences.
questions.answer:
Adjectives from the text:
1. healthy - Regular exercise and a balanced diet keep a person healthy.
2. large - A large crowd had gathered outside the stadium to watch the final match.
3. younger - My younger brother loves to play cricket in the evening.
4. painful - Losing a close friend is a very painful experience.
5. perplexed - The students looked perplexed when the teacher asked such a difficult question.
6. hygienic - Keeping our surroundings clean and hygienic protects us from many diseases.
7. organic - Farmers in our village grow organic vegetables without using chemical fertilisers.
8. polluted - Drinking water from a polluted stream can make you seriously ill.
9. positive - A positive attitude helps us face difficult situations with courage.

Adverbs from the text:
10. eagerly - The children waited eagerly for the school picnic to begin.
11. quietly - She quietly closed the door so that she would not disturb her sleeping father.
12. excitedly - The team members talked excitedly about their victory in the tournament.
13. properly - You must wash your hands properly with soap before eating food.
14. hardly - He had hardly reached the station when the train left.
questions.explanation: Adjectives describe nouns (healthy habits, a large crowd) while adverbs describe verbs, adjectives or other adverbs, often ending in '-ly' (wash properly, talk excitedly). The task requires identifying both kinds from the passage and then using them in original sentences.

questions.question: Task 2: Based on the information shared in the textbook and using other resources, organize a declamation contest on one of the following topics: (a) A hand washed is a life saved (b) Water - it takes a community to save children (c) Science and Tradition: can they be combined?
questions.answer:
A declamation contest is a contest in which speakers deliver a prepared speech on a given topic with feeling and expression. Here is a model speech for each topic that the class may use:

Topic (a) 'A hand washed is a life saved':
Respected judges, teachers and my dear friends. Today I want to remind you of something so simple that we often take it for granted - washing our hands. Diarrhoea and many other infections spread from germs that travel from our hands into our mouths. Yet a single wash with soap and clean water, done at the right moments, can stop these germs in their tracks. The World Health Organization calls handwashing the cheapest 'vaccine' in the world. If each of us washes our hands before eating and after using the toilet, we do not only protect ourselves but also our families and classmates. Truly, a hand washed is a life saved.

Topic (b) 'Water - it takes a community to save children':
Dear audience, we all know that clean water is life. But in our country only about 12 per cent of households use treated water, while the rest drink water that may be contaminated. Dirty water causes diarrhoea, which is one of the main causes of death among young children. No single person can solve this problem alone. It takes a whole community - parents, teachers, neighbours and the government - to protect the village well, to boil drinking water, to stop open defecation and to keep water sources clean. When the community works together, our children survive and grow up strong.

Topic (c) 'Science and Tradition: can they be combined?':
Honourable judges, some people believe that science and tradition are enemies. I believe they are good friends. Dada Jaan's generation had no factory-made soap, yet they used alum (phitkari), turmeric, neem leaves and camphor, all of which modern science now confirms are antiseptic and antibacterial. Science does not replace our traditions; it explains and improves them. When we add a scientist's knowledge to a grandmother's wisdom, we get the best of both worlds. So yes - science and tradition can, and must, be combined.

Preparation steps: (i) divide the class into teams, (ii) choose one topic per speaker, (iii) research supporting facts and statistics, (iv) prepare a 3-4 minute speech, (v) practise delivery, pauses and gestures, and (vi) hold the contest with a panel of judges.
questions.explanation: A declamation is a formal speech delivered from memory with expression. The passage supplies the themes (handwashing, water contamination and WASH awareness, and traditional versus modern science), which the students must research further and present.

questions.question: Task 3: Talk to your parents, teachers and community members, and if you have access to a library or the internet use those sources to collect information on the following: (1) What are the main sources of drinking water in your residence area/neighbourhood? (2) How does water get contaminated? (3) Are there any visible signs of water contamination or unhygienic practices near the source of drinking water? List them down. (4) What are the common ways of purifying or cleaning water?
questions.answer:
A model report based on community enquiry:

(1) Main sources of drinking water: In most neighbourhoods the main sources are: tap water supplied by the municipal or town authority; hand pumps and tube wells; water tankers that deliver water to homes; open wells in older or rural areas; and bottled or filtered water from shops. In villages, canal water and underground tube wells are the chief sources.

(2) How water gets contaminated: Water is contaminated when (i) sewage lines leak into water-supply pipes; (ii) open defecation near a well or stream allows germs to enter; (iii) garbage, animal waste or industrial chemicals are dumped into canals and streams; (iv) animals are bathed or watered in the same pond that people use; (v) storage tanks and pitchers are left uncovered so dust, insects and hands touch the water; and (vi) agricultural pesticides and fertilisers run off into surface water.

(3) Visible signs of contamination and unhygienic practices: muddy or brownish, cloudy water; a bad smell or taste; floating garbage, plastic and animal waste near the source; broken or leaking pipes; uncovered storage tanks and water pitchers; standing stagnant water breeding mosquitoes; people washing clothes, animals or utensils at the drinking-water point; open drains flowing beside hand pumps; and the absence of soap and clean water near the toilet.

(4) Common ways of purifying/cleaning water: boiling the water for at least ten minutes; filtering through ceramic or candle filters; chlorinating with bleaching powder or tablets; solar disinfection (leaving water in clear bottles in sunlight); distilling; using packaged or reverse-osmosis (RO) purified water; and simple household practices such as covering stored water, using a clean long-handled mug, and washing storage containers regularly.
questions.explanation: This is a community-based research task. The answer follows the four sub-questions in order and combines what the passage teaches about WASH (Water, Sanitation and Hygiene) with information gathered from family, teachers, the library and the internet.

questions.section: Unit 8 You are what you eat
questions.question: Task 1: Explore the effects of stunting on young children by using resources available to you, including local medical staff or a doctor, the internet, the science textbook or other reading materials.
questions.answer:
A research report on stunting:

Meaning: Stunting is the condition in which a child is too short for his or her age because of long-term poor nutrition and repeated illness. The science textbook, a local doctor and the passage 'You are what you eat' all support the same conclusions.

Effects on young children:
1. Physical growth: Stunted children have low height for their age because malnutrition in the early years causes irreversible damage to physical growth.
2. Brain development: A shortage of protein, iron and iodine harms mental development, resulting in poor memory, lower intelligence and weak concentration.
3. Weak immunity: Such children fall ill more often and recover slowly from infections, which further worsens their nutrition.
4. Lower school performance: Poor concentration, low energy and frequent absences lead to weak results and, later, to a higher chance of dropping out.
5. Reduced earning capacity: As adults, stunted children are less productive and earn less, which keeps families trapped in poverty.
6. Risk of other diseases: Stunting is linked to mood swings, low blood pressure, anaemia and other physical and mental disorders later in life.

Key facts from the book: In Pakistan, 1 in 4 children of five years and below is stunted, and Sindh has a stunting rate of 45.5 per cent, which is higher than the national average.

Prevention: A balanced diet with all food groups, exclusive breastfeeding, timely introduction of soft food around five months, clean water, handwashing, and low-cost nutritious foods such as moringa (sahajna) leaves and tea.
questions.explanation: Stunting results from chronic malnutrition in the early years and causes permanent short height. The book gives the alarming statistics (1 in 4 children nationally, 45.5 per cent in Sindh) that make this research task important.

questions.section: Unit 8 You are what you eat
questions.question: Task 2: List down 5 idioms, similes or phrases that have a food reference (e.g. 'Apple of one's eye'). Write down their meaning and use them in a sentence.
questions.answer:
1. Apple of one's eye - a person who is loved very much / a great favourite. Sentence: The youngest child is the apple of her grandmother's eye.

2. Bread and butter - the main source of a person's income or livelihood. Sentence: Selling cloth at the local market is the family's bread and butter.

3. In hot water - in serious trouble. Sentence: After missing three homework assignments, the boy found himself in hot water with his teacher.

4. As cool as a cucumber - very calm and relaxed, especially in a difficult situation. Sentence: Even before her final match, Ayesha was as cool as a cucumber.

5. The apple doesn't fall far from the tree - a child usually behaves or looks like his or her parents. Sentence: Like his father, Ali loves poetry - the apple doesn't fall far from the tree.
questions.explanation: Food references are common in English idioms, similes and proverbs. Each phrase here is explained with its meaning and then shown in a complete sentence, as the task requires.

questions.section: Unit 8 You are what you eat
questions.question: Task 3: What is the place that you would like to go and visit? What would you like to experience over there? Make a five-minute presentation in the class to share your plans.
questions.answer:
A model five-minute presentation:

'Good morning, respected teacher and my dear classmates. Today I will share the details of one place I have always dreamt of visiting - the magnificent northern valley of Hunza in Gilgit-Baltistan.

What I would like to see and experience:
1. The scenery: I want to see the snowy peaks of Rakaposhi and the Passu cones, the blue Attabad Lake and the green terraced fields against the white mountains.
2. The people and culture: I want to sit with the warm and hospitable Hunza people, learn a few words of their language and taste their local apricot dishes and apricot tea.
3. Adventure: I hope to trek on the Baltit and Altit fort trails, cross a hanging bridge and, if possible, walk a short distance on the Karakoram Highway.
4. History: I want to explore the centuries-old Baltit Fort and learn how people lived in these mountains long ago.
5. Health and routine: I want to experience the famous healthy lifestyle of Hunza, where people stay active and eat fresh, natural food every day.

Why this place: Hunza combines natural beauty, culture and healthy living, which matches everything we have been learning about in this unit.

My plan: I would travel in summer with my family, stay for about a week, travel by bus or by air to Gilgit and then by road, and keep a small journal and camera to record my experiences.

Thank you for listening; I would be happy to answer your questions.'
questions.explanation: This is an oral presentation task. A good presentation should name the place, describe what the speaker wishes to see and do, explain the reason for the choice, and outline a simple travel plan, all within five minutes.

questions.section: Unit 8 You are what you eat
questions.question: Task 4 (part 1): During school recess and closing time, observe how many snacks are being sold by the vendors. Make a list of up to 10 food items and their prices, and ask the vendor what each food item is made of. Refer to your list and categorize the items into healthy and unhealthy snacks.
questions.answer:
Model survey list of snacks sold around the school (prices are approximate):

1. Samosa (Rs. 20) - made of flour (maida), potatoes, spices and oil for frying.
2. Pakora (Rs. 20) - gram flour (besan), onions, potatoes and spices, deep-fried in oil.
3. Fruit chaat (Rs. 40) - fresh apples, bananas, guavas, oranges, lemon juice and chaat masala.
4. Boiled potatoes / chana chaat (Rs. 30) - boiled chickpeas, potato, onion, tomato, lemon and spices.
5. Cold drink / soft drink bottle (Rs. 60) - aerated water, sugar, artificial colour and flavouring.
6. Chocolate and candies (Rs. 10-50) - sugar, cocoa, milk solids, colour and preservatives.
7. Chips and crisps packets (Rs. 20-50) - potato slices fried in palm oil with a lot of salt and flavourings.
8. Biscuits and cream rolls (Rs. 10-40) - refined flour, sugar, hydrogenated fat and cream.
9. Roasted corn (bhutta) (Rs. 40) - fresh corn, salt, lemon and a little butter.
10. Fresh juice or lassi (Rs. 40) - fresh fruit or yoghurt, water and sugar.

Categorization:
Healthy snacks: fruit chaat, boiled chana/potato chaat, roasted corn (bhutta), fresh juice or lassi - these give vitamins, minerals, fibre and protein.
Unhealthy snacks: samosa, pakora, soft drinks, chocolates and candies, chips and crisps, cream biscuits - these are high in oil, sugar and salt and low in nutrients.
questions.explanation: The task combines observation with nutrition knowledge from the passage 'You are what you eat'. Healthy snacks are low in oil, sugar and salt and rich in nutrients, while fried, sugary and packaged snacks are unhealthy.

questions.section: Unit 8 You are what you eat
questions.question: Task 4 (part 2): Together identify two unhealthy snacks that are being sold around the school, then make a campaign poster to be displayed outside the school showing the harmful effects of eating that unhealthy food and suggesting healthy alternatives.
questions.answer:
Two unhealthy snacks sold around the school: (1) samosa/pakora (deep-fried in reused oil) and (2) cold drinks and chips packets (high sugar and salt).

Model campaign poster:

Headline: STOP! THINK BEFORE YOU SNACK!

Sub-heading: Two snacks are harming our students - fried samosas/pakoras and sugary cold drinks and chips.

Harmful effects of fried snacks and soft drinks:
- They are cooked in reused oil and contain a lot of fat, salt and sugar.
- They cause obesity, stomach upsets, food poisoning and later heart disease and diabetes.
- They fill the stomach with 'empty calories' while giving almost no vitamins, minerals or protein.
- Constant eating of such food causes poor concentration, tooth decay and low energy in class.

Choose these healthy alternatives instead:
- Fresh fruit chaat, apples, bananas and guavas.
- Boiled chana or roasted bhutta.
- Fresh juice, lassi or clean drinking water instead of soft drinks.
- Roasted or baked snacks instead of deep-fried ones.

Slogan: 'Eat clean, stay keen - healthy snacks keep you lean!'

(Design note: use bright colours, a large 'STOP' sign, simple drawings of a fruit and a chip packet, and display the poster at the school gate.)
questions.explanation: A campaign poster must catch attention, name the problem snack, list its harmful effects and give healthy alternatives. The harmful effects and healthy choices are drawn from the nutrition lessons in the passage.

questions.section: Unit 8 You are what you eat
questions.question: Task 4 (part 3): Based on your research, write a letter to the editor on 'Healthy and Nutritious Meals for School-age Children'.
questions.answer:
Examination Hall,
Karachi.
15th January, 2026.

The Editor,
Daily Dawn,
Karachi.

Subject: Healthy and Nutritious Meals for School-age Children

Sir,

Through the columns of your esteemed newspaper, I wish to draw the attention of the authorities and parents towards the poor eating habits of school-age children.

A recent survey that my classmates and I carried out around our school showed that most students spend their pocket money on fried snacks, chips, candies and sugary cold drinks sold by street vendors. These foods are high in oil, salt and sugar and almost empty of vitamins and minerals. The result is that many of our children are overweight or, on the other hand, stunted, and they often complain of tiredness, stomach problems and poor concentration in class. According to health sources, one out of every four children in Pakistan under five years of age is stunted, and Sindh has a stunting rate as high as 45.5 per cent.

The solution is neither expensive nor difficult. Schools should ban the sale of unhealthy snacks and provide canteens that offer fresh fruit, boiled gram, roasted corn, milk, lassi and clean drinking water. Parents should pack a simple home-cooked lunch instead of giving money for junk food, and teachers should hold short awareness sessions on the food groups - vegetables and fruits, dairy, fibre, and meat and poultry. The government, too, can play its part by regulating the quality of food sold near schools.

If home, school and society work together, we can give every child a healthy start in life. I hope your newspaper will highlight this important issue.

Yours faithfully,
A. Student.
Class IX,
Government School, Karachi.
questions.explanation: The letter follows the standard format: sender's address, date, receiver's address, subject, salutation, body and closing. It states the problem, gives supporting facts from the research and the textbook, and suggests practical solutions.
